item.title: Riders stage safety protest before start of Giro di Lombardia
item.description: Riders at the Giro di Lombardia staged a five-minute protest before the start of Saturday's race to highlight growing safety concerns following a series of incidents involving race vehicles, the tournament organisers said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Riders at the Giro di Lombardia staged a five-minute protest before the start of Saturday's race to highlight growing safety concerns following a series of incidents involving race vehicles, the tournament organisers said. The protest came days after riders Thomas Gloag and Marcel Camprubi were struck by a police motorcycle travelling in the opposite direction during Tre Valli Varesine. "At the start of Il Lombardia, the riders came together to send an important message, stopping for five minutes to urge all road users to behave responsibly and show mutual respect, both during races and in everyday life," organisers RCS Sport said in a social media post. After organisers completed the start countdown, the peloton remained stationary, before Belgium's double Olympic champion Remco Evenepoel stepped forward to explain the riders' action. "There’s too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race," Evenepoel said. "Unfortunately we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us, so we want to make this statement to show to the world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or literally dying in what we like the most to do." Evenepoel was referring to the death of British cyclist Finlay [USN:L4N44B13Q TEXT:"Tarling"], younger brother of Ineos rider Josh Tarling, who was killed in a collision with a vehicle during the Tour of Portugal on August 14. The demonstration delayed the start of the final Monument race of the season by five minutes before the peleton set off. Reuters has contacted the International Cycling Union (UCI) for comment.

item.title: Philips wins Dutch court battle with shareholders over recall
item.description: A Dutch court on Saturday dismissed demands by shareholders of health technology company Philips for an investigation into allegations of misleading disclosures and management failures linked to the company's recall of sleep apnea devices.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A Dutch court on Saturday dismissed demands by shareholders of health technology company Philips (PHG.AS) for an investigation into allegations of misleading disclosures and management failures linked to the company's recall of sleep apnea devices. A large group of shareholders had [USN:L5N3VB062 TEXT:"demanded"] a court inquiry, as they said Philips executives had responded too late to the problems that led to the massive recall and had failed to adequately inform investors. Philips' shares lost about two thirds of their value when the company recalled around 15 million sleep apnea devices in 2021, after discovering that the foam in the machines could release harmful substances and might pose health risks. The Enterprise Chamber of the Amsterdam Court of Appeal in its ruling said it had found no indication that Philips had known about the problems long before it issued any warning. It also said there was no reason to assume executives should have intervened earlier at the Respironics subsidiary that made the devices. Philips had denied the accusations made by the shareholders and said it welcomed the court's decision. The sleep apnea devices recall led to probes in multiple countries, including France, where prosecutors are still investigating charges of aggravated fraud and failure to report safety risks. Philips in 2024 agreed to pay $1.1 billion to settle all personal injury claims related to the devices filed in the US.

item.title: La India detiene a cientos e impone un confinamiento en Delhi para impedir protestas
item.description: La policía detuvo el sábado en Delhi a cientos de manifestantes y al fundador del movimiento juvenil "Cucarachas", mientras las fuerzas de seguridad cerraban al tráfico algunas zonas de la capital para impedir una manifestación en la que se exigía la dimisión del presidente de la Comisión Electoral de la India.
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Sharma, Sunil Kataria, Sakshi Dayal
item.content:encoded: La policía detuvo el sábado en Delhi a cientos de manifestantes y al fundador del movimiento juvenil "Cucarachas", mientras las fuerzas de seguridad cerraban al tráfico algunas zonas de la capital para impedir una manifestación en la que se exigía la dimisión del presidente de la Comisión Electoral de la India. Miles de agentes de policía y personal paramilitar se desplegaron por toda la ciudad, se suspendieron los servicios de Internet móvil en el distrito financiero central y se cerraron decenas de estaciones de metro y mercados, mientras las autoridades tomaban medidas para impedir una concentración organizada por el movimiento "Cucarachas". La protesta iba dirigida contra el presidente de la Comisión Electoral, Gyanesh Kumar, por una revisión de las listas electorales que, según los críticos, beneficia de manera desproporcionada al Partido Bharatiya Janata (BJP) del primer ministro Narendra Modi. El movimiento tenía previsto reunir a miles de personas en Jantar Mantar, un lugar designado para las protestas en el centro de Delhi. Sin embargo, las fuerzas de seguridad acordonaron la zona antes de que comenzara la manifestación. No obstante, hubo pequeñas protestas en otros puntos de la ciudad, entre ellos un popular mercado de artesanía y el monumento al líder del movimiento por la libertad Mahatma Gandhi, donde los manifestantes corearon consignas exigiendo la dimisión de Kumar. "¡Viva la revolución!", coreaban algunos jóvenes manifestantes en el centro de Delhi mientras la policía los perseguía y arrastraba a decenas de ellos a los autobuses para llevárselos, pese a que más seguían llegando, según un testigo de Reuters. "Esto supone una violación de los derechos del pueblo y el país ya no lo va a tolerar más", dijo Yogendra Solanki a Reuters mientras la policía se lo llevaba escoltado. La policía también detuvo al fundador del Partido del Pueblo Cucaracha, Abhijeet Dipke, y a Saurav Das y Ashutosh Ranka, otros de sus líderes, cuando su vuelo procedente de Bombay aterrizó en Delhi, informó el grupo en un comunicado. DELHI, EN CONFINAMIENTO PARA IMPEDIR LAS PROTESTAS Las imágenes de televisión mostraban a Dipke desafiando a los agentes que se le acercaban a bordo del avión. "He venido para que me detengan, deténganme (…) No les tengo miedo", dijo. "No, esto no es una detención", respondió uno de los agentes. "Por favor, coopere". El movimiento condenó lo que calificó de "detención autoritaria" de sus líderes, exigió su liberación inmediata y dijo que la protesta continuaría de todos modos. Según mostraron los canales de televisión, también fueron detenidos algunos diputados de la oposición y exministros. La policía no hizo ningún comentario inmediato sobre las detenciones. En toda la extensa capital, con unos 20 millones de habitantes, las fuerzas de seguridad instalaron controles en las principales carreteras y en los puntos de acceso a la ciudad. Agentes de policía subieron a los autobuses en busca de manifestantes, mientras que los vehículos fueron sometidos a inspecciones. Las barricadas y los bloques de hormigón interrumpieron el tráfico, mientras que en las vías principales se apostaron vehículos antidisturbios equipados con lanzadores de gas lacrimógeno. NUEVO RETO PARA MODI Las manifestaciones suponen una de las pruebas más serias hasta la fecha para Modi, a raíz de las acusaciones de que las autoridades electorales revisaron indebidamente los censos electorales antes de las recientes elecciones estatales. Las protestas han cobrado impulso desde la semana pasada, cuando el periódico Indian Express informó de que dos comisionados electorales habían cuestionado y mostrado su desacuerdo con Kumar por las revisiones, que eliminaron aproximadamente 130 millones de nombres de las listas electorales. Kumar no ha hecho declaraciones al respecto, pero la Comisión Electoral y el BJP han negado las acusaciones de irregularidades. El BJP dijo que su éxito electoral refleja la popularidad de Modi y el crecimiento económico de la India, y acusa a los partidos de la oposición de difundir información errónea porque no han logrado ganar las elecciones. No obstante, las protestas casi a diario, suponen un nuevo reto para Modi, apenas unos meses después de que las manifestaciones por las filtraciones de exámenes obligaron a su ministro de Educación a dimitir. Los disturbios se producen además en vísperas de una serie de importantes elecciones estatales que comenzarán a principios de 2027. Las restricciones del sábado demostraron que el Gobierno de Modi ha "declarado oficialmente la guerra a su propio pueblo", dijo K.C. Venugopal, uno de los principales líderes del Partido del Congreso, el principal de la oposición. El portavoz del BJP, Sambit Patra, dijo que la democracia había prevalecido sobre el dominio de las turbas.

item.title: Singapore not ideal for sprints, say Hamilton and Verstappen
item.description: Singapore's Formula One circuit needs re-designing and lacks entertainment value for a sprint race, Saturday's sprint winner Max Verstappen and runner-up Lewis Hamilton said after the 20-lap race involved little overtaking.
item.dc:creator: Tom Westbrook
item.content:encoded: Singapore's Formula One circuit needs re-designing and lacks entertainment value for a sprint race, Saturday's sprint winner Max Verstappen and runner-up Lewis Hamilton said after the 20-lap race involved little overtaking. Rain delayed the start of the inaugural sprint at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, and with overtaking nearly impossible the only drama came in the form of collisions and a record nine retirements. "I think we shouldn't host a sprint where you can't pass," Red Bull's polesitter Verstappen told reporters after notching his [USN:L1N45W02M TEXT:"first victory"] at the circuit. "I'm fine, I just do my thing... but it's not what I like. The overtake mode, it barely does anything here. You don't really gain a lot on the straights ... we need to have a longer straight or like more of a proper hairpin to overtake." Mercedes' George Russell spun into the wall on the final turn of the first lap when he was leading the sprint while the two McLaren cars collided on the last lap while chasing the final podium spot. SAFETY CAR In between, six of the 20 laps ran behind a safety car, which is commonplace in Singapore due to crashes, while 11 of the 16 race wins have come from pole position. "I love the race here, (but) I was just saying to Max, I think they need to change the track to maybe a longer straight somewhere in order to allow it to be truly a great racing circuit," Hamilton said. "It's a great track to drive over a single lap and qualifying, but ... there's like one place, really, that you could potentially get close to overtaking. "I thought it was fun, but if it was dry, that would have been probably the most boring race for you to have watched. It was the rain, that made it exciting." Reduced distance sprint races, with eight points going to the winner, are held on Saturdays with sprint qualifying replacing the usual second Friday practice sessions. Singapore's was the sixth and final sprint race this season and it is not on next year's 10-event sprint calendar, though another city circuit in Monaco is on the schedule -- a venue Ferrari's hometown hero Charles Leclerc said was not ideal. "I don't think it makes sense to have any sprint races on city tracks in general," said Leclerc, who finished third in Singapore's sprint. "Here or Monaco, I don't think it adds anything to the weekend."

item.title: Ducks ride versatile offense into encounter vs. winless Flames
item.description: The Anaheim Ducks arrive in Calgary to face the struggling Flames on Saturday night with a level of confidence beyond having won three of four games to start the season.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The Anaheim Ducks arrive in Calgary to face the struggling Flames on Saturday night with a level of confidence beyond having won three of four games to start the season. The Ducks are flying high with the knowledge they can pull off a victory without offensive contributions from their biggest guns. Anaheim comes to Calgary after a decisive 5-1 win at the Winnipeg Jets on Friday in a game in which the difference makers were fourth-line players. Judd Caulfield, Tim Washe and Jeff Malott all recorded their first career multi-point game. Caulfield, 25, scored his first NHL goal. "They had a special night," Ducks coach Joel Quenneville said. "They scored a couple off the rush, almost had a third one off the rush, had a couple shifts in the third with good possession and cycle time. We couldn't ask for anything more." Anaheim's Beckett Sennecke notched a pair of assists, giving him six points (three goals, three assists) in a four-game point streak to start the season. Leo Carlsson and Cutter Gauthier, however, were scoreless on Friday. It was a non-issue with the lower-profile players stepping up to hand Winnipeg its first regulation-time loss of the season. "It feels great to get that first one," Caulfield said of his first big-league tally. "It was a great play by Washe to get that puck out of the zone and (Malott) had great speed taking the puck to the net and left it easy for me to score." After Lukas Dostal started in goal in Winnipeg, expect Ville Husso to start at the position for Anaheim on Saturday. The Flames, the only NHL team without a point, are trying to find any spark in the early going. Calgary, which is coming off a 7-3 loss to the Colorado Avalanche on Thursday, has lost all four of its games this season, by a combined score of 23-6. As lopsided as the results have been, including the loss to Colorado, there is a belief that Thursday's game was a step forward for Calgary. "In the first (period), I thought we played with some energy and pace and created a lot of chances," captain Mikael Backlund said. "It's obviously really tough and hard and frustrating to lose again. We've got to learn from it, find a way to play a really solid 60 (minutes). We haven't done that yet, and it's time we do that on Saturday." As much as the Flames are struggling offensively, there is a strong thought that their fortunes will change if they improve defensively. All four losses have been blowouts, and the goaltending duo of Dustin Wolf and Devin Cooley believe they must find a way to make a difference and help their teammates find momentum. "We've given up too many goals; that's the bottom line," Wolf said. "I think sometimes we can laugh about it, but our objective is to get points, and we're not doing a good enough job -- I'm not doing a good enough job -- of helping our team do that." The Pacific Division rivals will meet again Tuesday night in Anaheim, Calif., in the second game of a home-and-home series. --Field Level Media

item.title: Verstappen se lleva su primera victoria de la temporada en una carrera al sprint caótica en Singapur
item.description: Max Verstappen, de Red Bull, saboreó la victoria en Singapur por primera vez en la temporada. El piloto neerlandés, que partió desde la "pole", se impuso en una caótica carrera al sprint, tras un retraso de más de 30 minutos en la salida debido a las fuertes lluvias y en la que nueve autos abandonaron la carrera, lo que supone un récord para este tipo de competencia.
item.dc:creator: Rohith Nair
item.content:encoded: Max Verstappen, de Red Bull, saboreó la victoria en Singapur por primera vez en la temporada. El piloto neerlandés, que partió desde la "pole", se impuso en una caótica carrera al sprint, tras un retraso de más de 30 minutos en la salida debido a las fuertes lluvias y en la que nueve autos abandonaron la carrera, lo que supone un récord para este tipo de competencia. Verstappen cruzó la línea de meta por delante de Lewis Hamilton y Charles Leclerc, ambos de Ferrari. "Quiero ganar mañana. No considero esto una victoria en el sentido de haber ganado realmente un Gran Premio", dijo Verstappen. El líder del campeonato de Mercedes, Kimi Antonelli, se hizo con el cuarto puesto tras una colisión entre los dos McLaren en la última vuelta, mientras que su compañero de equipo, George Russell, sufrió un accidente cuando iba en cabeza en la primera vuelta. Verstappen había conservado su "pole position" tras librarse de una sanción por adelantar bajo bandera amarilla el viernes, pero el holandés tuvo una salida lenta, mientras que Russell se ponía en cabeza y Hamilton remontaba rápidamente del sexto al tercer puesto. La escapada de Russell terminó en la última curva de la primera vuelta, cuando su neumático trasero se subió al bordillo y derrapó contra el muro, lo que provocó la salida del auto de seguridad. "La salida volvió a ser horrible, así que sin duda es algo en lo que tenemos que mejorar, porque si mañana ocurre algo así, se acaba la carrera a menos que pase alguna locura", añadió Verstappen. "Después de eso, lo único que quieres es mantener la calma y el control, porque sabes que aquí no se puede adelantar". "UN ERROR TONTO" DE RUSSELL Russell explicó que un error de cálculo le hizo derrapar en la última curva. "Al salir de la curva, tenía más consumo de batería del que pensaba. Me empujó un poco más hacia fuera de lo que esperaba y entonces me salí por la línea blanca", explicó Russell. "Sí, un error tonto. Con consecuencias muy, muy graves". La carnicería continuó cuando Lance Stroll y Sergio Pérez se retiraron tras chocar entre sí, y a Isack Hadjar, de Red Bull, se le pidió detener su auto debido a un problema técnico. El vehículo de seguridad permaneció en pista después de que el Alpine de Franco Colapinto también se detuvo, y la carrera no se reanudó hasta la séptima vuelta. Verstappen lideraba por delante de los Ferrari de Hamilton y Leclerc, mientras que los McLaren de Oscar Piastri y Lando Norris se situaban entre los cinco primeros, por delante de Antonelli. Sin embargo, las esperanzas de McLaren de subir al podio se desvanecieron cuando el vigente campeón Norris rozó a Piastri y ambos coches hicieron un trompo, lo que permitió a Antonelli ascender al cuarto puesto y ampliar su ventaja en el campeonato sobre Russell a 89 puntos. "Miré por los retrovisores y vi las luces rojas de la parte trasera de los McLaren. Así que supe que había pasado algo", explicó Leclerc. La sesión de clasificación para la carrera del domingo se retrasó debido a la lluvia.

item.title: Norris apologises after collision dashes McLaren sprint hopes
item.description: World champion Lando Norris apologised to his McLaren team after a final-lap collision with team mate Oscar Piastri wrecked their pursuit of a podium finish at a chaotic Singapore Grand Prix sprint on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Rohith Nair
item.content:encoded: World champion Lando Norris apologised to his McLaren team after a final-lap collision with team mate Oscar Piastri wrecked their pursuit of a podium finish at a [USN:L1N45W02M TEXT:"chaotic Singapore Grand Prix sprint"] on Saturday. The McLaren duo were chasing Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who was struggling with his tyres in the dying stages of the 20-lap sprint, when disaster struck on the final lap. Norris, running fifth behind Piastri in fourth, attempted to overtake his team mate but clipped the Australian's rear tyre with his front wheel, sending both cars spinning and handing Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli fourth place. "Sorry about that. Obviously I didn't want that to happen but I thought I was fully alongside. I just ran out of space at the apex but I was there," Norris said over the team radio. While Norris limped home to eighth place to claim the final point available, Piastri was forced to retire as he became one of nine cars that did not finish - a record number of retirements for a Formula One sprint race. "I'd rather just go back and review it," Norris told Sky Sports. "I apologised to them that one of the cars is out but, like I said, the rest of it we'll go review." Piastri said he had not seen the incident properly to comment but downplayed its significance as they were not in high points scoring positions. "From where I sit, it's for fourth and fifth for a sprint race, so I'm not that bothered either way," Piastri said. "Just obviously it's a lot of work now for the team to get both cars fixed (ahead of qualifying for Sunday's race). Just a shame for the team." Both McLaren drivers were summoned to the stewards after the collision. Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the sprint and the Dutchman leapfrogged Norris to climb to fifth in the world championship standings.

item.title: Struggling Blues eager to ignite offense vs. Blue Jackets
item.description: The St. Louis Blues will look to halt a three-game losing streak when they host the Columbus Blue Jackets on Saturday night.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The St. Louis Blues will look to halt a three-game losing streak when they host the Columbus Blue Jackets on Saturday night. The Blues have hit sour notes following a 4-0 victory over the Dallas Stars in a season opener on Oct. 2. St. Louis fell 3-2 in overtime in its most recent outing, at home against the San Jose Sharks on Thursday. "I think we certainly felt like we gave ourselves an opportunity to win the game, so only coming away with one point is disappointing," Blues defenseman Cam Fowler said. "But there's a lot that we can build off of as well ... some points in our game that we can work on moving forward and getting ready for Saturday." St. Louis has just five goals during its winless stretch (0-2-1). Blues coach Jim Montgomery vented his frustration over the team's lack of goal scoring with a colorful quote following Thursday's loss. "Right now, if we fell out of a boat and we were trying to score a goal, we would not hit the ocean, and it's causing problems," he said. Connor McMichael and Dillon Dube each scored a goal for the Blues on Thursday. Off-season additions McMichael (two goals, two assists) and Mason McTavish (two goals, one assist) are leading the way offensively for the Blues, while captain Robert Thomas has failed to record a point through the first four games. Thomas has topped the Blues in points over each of the past two seasons and has 373 points in 361 games over his previous five seasons. The Blue Jackets should be feeling good heading into Saturday's game after outlasting the Pittsburgh Penguins 3-2 in a shootout on Friday. Kent Johnson scored the lone shootout goal to secure the victory. Damon Severson and Mathieu Olivier also found the back of the net in regulation for Columbus. The Blue Jackets controlled the majority of the play against the Penguins, outshooting them 45-22. "You saw a lot tonight how we wanna play; Columbus Blue Jacket hockey was out there tonight for the most part," Columbus coach Rick Bowness said. "We dominated the game at certain times, and yeah they had some flashes, they're an excellent hockey team over there. For the most part that's Columbus Blue Jackets hockey, we're going north, we're hard to play against. That was good to see." Severson, who was playing in his first game this season, also picked up an assist, and Cole Sillinger set up two goals in the win. Cam Talbot made 20 saves and denied all three attempts in the shootout en route to his first win in a Blue Jackets uniform. Talbot signed with the team as a free agent on a one-year, $950,000 deal last month. Columbus will play on the road for the first time this season on Saturday. The Blue Jackets have dominated the Blues in recent seasons, winning the previous six meetings. --Field Level Media

item.title: Major Saudi conferences to proceed, organisers say, despite deadly airport attack
item.description: The organisers of two major Saudi energy and investment conferences said their events will go ahead this month and reassured visitors on security, after missile attacks on Riyadh's airport left four people dead and an airliner heavily damaged this week.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni
item.content:encoded: The organisers of two major Saudi energy and investment conferences said their events will go ahead this month and reassured visitors on security, after [USN:L1N45V07H TEXT:"missile attacks"] on Riyadh's airport left four people dead and an airliner heavily damaged this week. The attacks led to widespread flight disruptions, with people taking land routes or circuitous alternative flights. The UK, France and Germany have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh. Riyadh is sticking to plans to convene global events and trying to draw in investment even amid escalating war with the Iran-backed Houthis in neighbouring Yemen that has seen the kingdom attacked dozens of times over the past weeks. Organisers of the World Petroleum Congress, set to host top global oil executives and policymakers from Sunday to Thursday, said it would proceed as planned with foreign leaders and ministers in attendance, an email sent to delegates said. "Your comfort is our priority," it said, noting that alternative routes to Riyadh, including via a four-hour drive from Dammam on the kingdom's eastern coast, were available. Italian Energy Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin on Friday said he would not fly to Riyadh for the International Energy Forum Ministerial Meeting, an event on WPC's sidelines, but would participate via video link. The Future Investment Initiative, launched by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman as the kingdom's flagship investment conference a decade ago, would also proceed as planned from October 26-29, organisers said. "Safety and well-being remain our highest priority," a statement attributed to FII CEO Maha Al Saud said. "Comprehensive security measures will be in place at Riyadh's airports, our conference venues and official hotels, with coordinated arrangements for participants' transportation," it said. Chief executives of some of the world's biggest financial institutions such as JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon and Citi's Jane Fraser were on the list of expected attendees. Citi and JPMorgan did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group earlier this month. Germany's Lufthansa has suspended Riyadh flights through October 16 while Gulf carriers Etihad Airways and Flydubai have cancelled flights to and from the Saudi capital scheduled for October 10. Saudi Arabia has responded to Houthi attacks with a wave of strikes on missile launcher sites, vowing to protect the kingdom, and says it has intercepted many ballistic missiles fired by the group.

item.title: China proposes stricter car design, testing rules, including ban on fully hidden door handles
item.description: China's industry ministry on Saturday proposed tighter oversight of automakers' innovative designs and research and development testing. It said some manufacturers had rushed out new models without enough validation, which raised safety and environmental risks.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: China's industry ministry on Saturday proposed tighter oversight of automakers' innovative designs and research and development testing. It said some manufacturers had rushed out new models without enough validation, which raised safety and environmental risks. • From January 1, 2027, automakers seeking approval for new models must submit more technical details on innovative designs and testing. Models that are poorly tested or backed by false data will be rejected, the draft said • Models that already have approval must file information on their innovative designs by July 1, 2027. If they do not and have safety hazards, automakers must halt production and recall them • The draft bans fully hidden door handles and foldable or flexible displays. It also bars use of "zero-gravity" or swivel seats while driving • Key functions such as lights and wipers must keep physical controls • The ministry drafted the rules with three other agencies and is taking public comment until November 10

item.title: EU's Irish presidency wants 8% cut to proposed 2028-2034 budget plan
item.description: The Irish EU presidency proposed on Saturday an 8% cut in the European Commission's budget plan for the period 2028 to 2034 to €1.6 trillion ($1.79 trillion), drawing criticism from more frugal member states that the reduction is not deep enough.
item.dc:creator: Jan Strupczewski, Yun Chee Foo
item.content:encoded: The Irish EU presidency proposed on Saturday an 8% cut in the European Commission's budget plan for the period 2028 to 2034 to €1.6 trillion ($1.79 trillion), drawing criticism from more frugal member states that the reduction is not deep enough. The Irish proposal still marks a 30% increase over the bloc's current budget, which runs from 2021 to 2027. The EU budget is the main source of financing for all of the 27-country bloc's main policies. The Commission, the EU executive, has said the bloc needs to spend more on defence and boosting European competitiveness, while some member states want to retain most of the expenditure to support farming and regional development. "The Negotiating Box provides savings of 8%, or €141 billion, on the Commission's original proposal," said Ireland, current holder of the EU's six-month rotating presidency, referring to its compromise proposal. Ireland put the Commission's original €2 trillion figure adjusted for inflation over the seven-year period at €1.76 trillion based on 2025 prices, which resulted in an 8% reduction. IRELAND SAYS PLAN SEEKS TO RECONCILE COMPETING DEMANDS "As we see it, the negotiating box acts to bridge the many differences between the member states," Irish minister Thomas Byrne told a press conference. "It brings us closer to resolving the budgetary trilemma, addressing the talks of how best to finance new priorities in competitiveness, research, innovation, security and defence while at the same time addressing core policies," he said. The proposal sets out a 3% cut in spending on regional development, agriculture and fisheries from the Commission's own figures — the biggest outlay in the budget — and a 13% reduction in spending on competitiveness and security. It foresees €55 billion in new financing options derived from customs duties, a share of the cash EU governments get from selling CO2 emissions permits to companies and an annual lump-sum contribution from large companies operating in the EU, among other sources. Sweden's minister for EU affairs, Jessica Rosencrantz, described the Irish proposal in a post on X as "wildly unaffordable", while Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen said his country could also not accept it. Both countries are part of a fiscally cautious group which wants budget cutbacks. However, lawmakers in the European Parliament, which wants a 10% increase in the Commission's €2 trillion proposal, said the Irish plan would weaken Europe and would not win their consent. EU leaders will discuss the Irish proposal in Brussels on October 15 to 16. The EU budget, which is known as the [USN:L8N41B114 TEXT:"Multiannual Financial Framework"], needs to be agreed by all 27 member states. ($1 = 0.8928 euros)

item.title: Israeli strikes kill five people in Gaza, medics say
item.description: Israeli strikes killed at least five Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in two separate attacks on Saturday, health officials said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Israeli strikes killed at least five Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in two separate attacks on Saturday, health officials said. Medics said an Israeli strike killed four people near Panda Mall in Gaza City, while another killed one person in the Tuffah neighbourhood further south of the city. The Israeli military said the two strikes targeted militants, without giving further information. Israel has stepped up strikes against Hamas in recent weeks, saying the Palestinian militant group has been rearming and carrying out attacks in violation of the ceasefire. Hamas denies rebuilding its arsenal or planning attacks and accuses Israel of undermining a US-brokered ceasefire agreed a year ago. The ceasefire calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made towards implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops. Gaza health officials have said at least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the truce was agreed last October. Israel says four of its soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza over the same period. The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led [USN:L1N45T04T TEXT:"October 7, 2023 attacks"] on Israel, which killed 1,200 people, while a further 251 were taken hostage. Israel's subsequent bombardment and ground operations in Gaza have killed more than 74,000 people, according to Gaza health officials.

item.title: Germany sticks to Russia sanctions after Trump announcement on diesel
item.description: Germany said on Saturday it would maintain sanctions against Russia over its war on Ukraine following US President Donald Trump's announcement that his administration had temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Germany said on Saturday it would maintain sanctions against Russia over its war on Ukraine following US President Donald Trump's announcement that his administration had temporarily [USN:L1N45V0MW TEXT:"lifted US sanctions"] on Russian fuel. "The federal government has taken note of the US decision relating to Russian diesel deliveries," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement. He said Germany's position remained clear: "The federal government remains committed to the decisions on sanctions against Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions." He said Germany's support for Ukraine was unchanged and diplomatic efforts to reach a solution would continue. Trump said on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices. He said his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. Prices for diesel, used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking, have risen to near record levels, posing a risk for Trump's fellow Republicans ahead of the November 3 congressional elections that will determine whether they maintain thin control of Congress. Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who visited Kyiv last weekend, has said repeatedly that Germany, Ukraine's largest European donor, would not reduce its support for the Kyiv government.

item.title: Palmer signs Chelsea contract until 2034
item.description: Chelsea attacking midfielder Cole Palmer has signed a contract extension to keep him at Stamford Bridge until 2034, the Premier League club said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Chelsea attacking midfielder Cole Palmer has signed a contract extension to keep him at Stamford Bridge until 2034, the Premier League club said on Saturday. The 24-year-old England international has become a key figure since joining Chelsea from Manchester City in 2023, scoring 91 goals in 138 appearances across all competitions. He was part of the squad that won the Club World Cup and UEFA Conference League. "Speaking to the owners, to the sporting directors and obviously the manager, they gave me a lot of confidence so it was only right to sign," Palmer said. "Speaking to players as well, everyone has the same ambitions. I feel like we win major trophies here consistently." Chelsea have agreed long-term contracts Chelsea with several first-team players and emerging talent. Forward [USN:L6N44J020 TEXT:"Joao Pedro"] recently signed a deal through 2034, and winger Pedro Neto agreed a six-year contract last month. Chelsea, 10th in the Premier League table, host Bournemouth on Saturday.

item.title: Verstappen claims first Singapore win as nine retirements mar chaotic sprint
item.description: Red Bull's Max Verstappen tasted victory in Singapore for the first time as the polesitter won a chaotic sprint on Saturday after the start was delayed by over 30 minutes due to heavy rain while nine cars retired, a record for sprint races.
item.dc:creator: Rohith Nair
item.content:encoded: Red Bull's Max Verstappen tasted victory in Singapore for the first time as the polesitter won a chaotic sprint on Saturday after the [USN:L1N45W02H TEXT:"start was delayed by over 30 minutes"] due to heavy rain while nine cars retired, a record for sprint races. The victory was the first of any kind for the Dutchman in Singapore as he took the chequered flag ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc. "I want to win tomorrow. I don't see this as a win in terms of actually winning a Grand Prix," Verstappen said. Mercedes' championship leader Kimi Antonelli was gifted fourth place after the two McLarens collided on the final lap while his team mate George Russell crashed out of the lead on lap one. Verstappen had kept his [USN:L1N45V0HG TEXT:"pole position"] after escaping a penalty for overtaking under a yellow flag on Friday but the Dutchman made a slow start as Russell stormed ahead and Hamilton swiftly moved up from sixth to third. Russell's sprint ended on the last turn of lap one when his rear tyre went over the kerb and he spun into the wall to bring the safety car out. "The start was horrendous again, so that's definitely something that we need to improve on because if you have something like that tomorrow, that's your race over if nothing crazy happens," Verstappen added. "After that, you just want to keep it calm and under control because you know that you can't pass around here." 'SILLY MISTAKE' FOR RUSSELL Russell said a miscalculation caused him to spin out at the last corner. "I came through the corner, had more battery deployment than I thought. Pushed me a little bit wider than I hoped and then I just went on the white line," Russell said. "Yeah, silly mistake. Big, big consequences." The carnage continued when Lance Stroll and Sergio Perez retired after they collided and Red Bull's Isack Hadjar was asked to stop his car due to a technical issue. The safety car remained on track after Franco Colapinto's Alpine also came to a standstill and they did not resume racing until lap seven. Verstappen led from the Ferraris of Hamilton and Leclerc while the McLarens of Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris were in the top five ahead of Antonelli. MCLARENS COLLIDE ON FINAL LAP McLaren's hopes of a podium vanished, however, when reigning champion Norris nudged into Piastri and the two cars spun out, allowing Antonelli to move up to fourth place and stretch his championship lead over Russell to 89 points. "I checked in my mirrors and I saw red lights of the back of the cars of the McLarens. So I knew that something happened," Leclerc said. The qualifying session for Sunday's race was delayed due to the rain.

item.title: Jocelyn Bioh on why Broadway is finally ready for ‘School Girls’
item.description: The playwright discusses what has changed since 'School Girls' was first produced, the universality of teenage insecurity and why bringing the play to Broadway feels like coming full circle.
item.dc:creator: Kathryn Lurie
item.content:encoded: Nearly a decade after Jocelyn Bioh wrote “School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play,” the play itself has barely changed. But the world around it has. The comedy about a group of teenage girls at a Ghanaian boarding school premiered off-Broadway in 2017, launching Bioh’s career as a playwright and going on to become a hit at regional theaters across the United States. But despite its success, Bioh was told it might not belong on Broadway. Now “School Girls” has made it there — following the Broadway success of Bioh’s “Jaja’s African Hair Braiding” in 2023 — and she is finding an audience that responds differently to the play’s exploration of body image, the privileging of lighter skin, known as colorism, and the often brutal social dynamics of girlhood. Beneath its rapid-fire jokes and teenage rivalries is a more painful story about who gets to be considered beautiful — and what people are willing to do to fit that ideal. Speaking in New York City, Bioh discusses what has changed since “School Girls” was first produced, the universality of teenage insecurity and why bringing the play to Broadway feels like coming full circle. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity. How does it feel to finally bring “School Girls” to Broadway? It feels incredibly humbling. This play changed my life. It was the first play of mine that ever got produced. I can very clearly mark what my life was like before opening night of that show and then after. That audiences and critics all still feel the same way nearly a decade later is a reminder that I was on the right track. It also feels doubly exciting because even though it had so much success regionally and has been all over the country, I was told, “It's a great play, but maybe it's not the right fit for a Broadway stage.” What do you think was meant by that, and what has changed enough for it to be on Broadway now? Broadway shows were very specific then. They didn't have ensembles that looked like the cast of “School Girls.” It was a lot of celebrities, a lot of things that seemed to fit into one specific category or box. The world has shifted. Audiences are different than they were 10 years ago. In a lot of ways, “Jaja's African Hair Braiding” having so much success was a marker that, a Broadway play is just a play that's on Broadway. It doesn't necessarily have to fit a specific category. Is there anything in the play that hits differently than it did when you first wrote it? The conversation around beauty standards and body image has shifted in the last 10 years. Some would say (for the) better, some would say worse, but we're all aware of it in a different way. The play kicks off with Paulina bullying Nana about her size and her eating. You can feel the audience is immediately on Nana's side. Halfway through the play, she has a moment where she really stands up to Paulina, and every night that moment gets applause. You can feel the audience cheering, almost jumping up ready to fight with her. They're taking off their earrings! We did not have that experience off-Broadway. I think we were in a time where we accepted the idea that if you were somebody who was bigger, you should be losing weight; you should be trying to conform. Our ideas of beauty are very different now. Big ships turn slow, but I appreciate that I can feel that in the audience. Did you rewrite much for this production? Very small things, little jokes that I thought would land better. But the play is still largely the same thing I wrote in 2016. If I were sitting down to write this play now, I don't know that I would be as honest or as vulnerable as I was then, particularly in the moments where Paulina is speaking very directly about how colorism has affected her life. I think I would censor myself a little bit now. I never thought the play would get produced, so I was very free and vulnerable in a way. Why? When you're a playwright and your name starts to grow within the community, you start to have an awareness of the responsibility of your words. And I'm okay with having that responsibility because I know I'm doing something really different. I'm really blowing open how people see Black and African people on a theatrical stage. There's an incredible responsibility to that. The play takes place in Ghana, but these girls feel instantly recognizable. Did you know when you were writing it how universal they would be? I understood that there's a real rich universality we have, particularly in school and friendship dynamics. Those things are evergreen and universal. I knew what I was writing was different, (that) the girls and the people I was reflecting were different, but I didn't want to alienate audiences. That's part of why I added the subtitle. What's something we all know and recognize about the teenage experience? Mean girls. Paulina seems to believe that if she can just become Miss Ghana, she can escape the limits of her life. Is her obsession with beauty really an obsession with power and possibility? Probably. Ultimately, I think she really believes this is going to set her up for a successful life in entertainment. The play is set in 1986, and if you became Miss Ghana, Miss World, Miss Universe — any of those things — you could become a star. This is how we have Vanessa Williams or Halle Berry or Kenya Moore, if you're of the “Real Housewives” persuasion. (Another character,) Eloise, is a former Miss Ghana and did leave. She's come back now living a different life, (signifying that) in order to have success, you've got to get out. In order to have power, you have to get out. Maybe Paulina doesn't see the beauty and power that she can build in her own country. That's reflective of so many immigrant, particularly African immigrant, stories: In order to have success, you need to leave. I don't know if the play were set in 2026, (if) that would be the case now. I think the play would be very different. But for Paulina and her circumstances then, that is what she believed. The play deals so directly with colorism. Do you think colorism is in some ways more sensitive to talk about than racism? They're inextricably linked. The play largely talks about and shows the effects of colorism, but then ends with a global lesson on racism. And we've not moved on from it. When we started rehearsals for the play in August, the biggest news story was Lupita Nyong'o playing Helen of Troy in Christopher Nolan's film (“The Odyssey”). (Her casting) did not fit with whomever's standard of beauty (for) the woman whose face launched a thousand ships. Why didn't it fit? Why were there so many suggestions about, “Well, Zendaya's in the movie, why can't she play that part?” That's a very clear conversation about colorism, whether people are using that word or not. When I wrote this play, it was really important for me to have that conversation because it had affected my life so much. Revisiting it now, especially in relation to these conversations that are happening globally, I'm like, well, we've not moved on from it. We can't move on from colorism because nobody's moved on from racism. I can't change people's minds. But if people come to see “School Girls” and their implicit bias can shift just a little bit, then I've done my job. The play is extremely funny until you realize how much pain is sitting underneath the humor. How deliberate is that? I really believe that comedy is just a funny way of being serious. Humor and pain are on two different sides of a truth coin. It's all rooted in truth. Paulina is a girl in the world who's trying to be affirmed and validated that she belongs there, that her beauty is widely accepted even if she knows that it's not. The lengths she goes to get there are what's comical, but it's rooted in something real that we all experience. At the end of the day, I'm a comedic writer and I want people to be entertained. But because I know the responsibility of who I'm introducing and the culture I'm introducing, I think there's a responsibility in also educating people. If I can make that medicine go down with a little bit of sugar, honey, agave, whatever you like, I'm willing to go there. item.title: Amelia Earhart expedition heads to Pacific atoll hoping to find her plane
item.description: A US-based team of marine archaeologists has set sail for a tiny island in the far western Pacific seeking to examine the latest tantalizing clue to one of the 20th century's great unsolved mysteries: the 1937 disappearance of famed aviator Amelia Earhart.
item.dc:creator: Steve Gorman
item.content:encoded: A US-based team of marine archaeologists has set sail for a tiny island in the far western Pacific seeking to examine the latest tantalizing clue to one of the 20th century's great unsolved mysteries: the 1937 disappearance of famed aviator Amelia Earhart. Backed by Purdue University, an institution long affiliated with Earhart and her legacy, the group aims to learn whether a submerged object detected by satellite imagery in the island's lagoon six years ago is the wreckage of Earhart's twin-engine Lockheed Electra 10-E airplane. Such a finding would conclusively prove the hypothesis of some scholars that Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, crash-landed on or near the coral-ringed atoll and perished as castaways there, hundreds of miles from their intended refueling stop. After embarking from Los Angeles earlier this month, the group was expected to arrive on Tuesday, October 13, local time at Nikumaroro, an uninhabited speck of land in the remote Phoenix Islands, part of the archipelago nation of the Kiribati Republic. "Finding Amelia Earhart's Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime," Richard Pettigrew, head of the Archaeological Legacy Institute in Eugene, Oregon, who is leading the effort in conjunction with Purdue, said in press materials for the mission. Purdue general counsel and expedition member Steve Schultz, who was in Fiji conducting advance work for the expedition last week, said in an interview: "This would be solving one of the great mysteries in aviation history, certainly one of the great mysteries of the 20th century," The mission has its skeptics. Chief among them is rival Earhart explorer Ric Gillespie, co-founder of TIGHAR, short for The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, and author of the 2024 "One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy." TREE OR PLANE? Gillespie has led a dozen expeditions of his own to the atoll over three decades and is the leading proponent of the Nikumaroro castaway theory. But he predicted the Pettigrew-Purdue team would find no airplane wreckage or anything else of consequence left on the island. The Purdue team credits Gillespie for laying the foundation of the theory they hope to prove. And they cite a compelling body of evidence that he has amassed over the years, including human artifacts recovered on the island, such as a 1930s-era glass cosmetic jar for freckle cream and remnants of a jackknife like one Earhart carried on the plane. Gillespie's investigation also encompassed modern forensic analysis from records of measurements of skeletal remains found on the island in the 1940s; logs of radio transmission bearings from distress calls picked up by wireless operators in the days immediately after Earhart vanished; and a photograph taken of the island's shoreline months later showing an object that Gillespie said appears to be the Electra's landing gear. In a Reuters interview last week, Gillespie said he believes the plane has since been lost to history, eventually swept by tides off the coral flat where it had landed largely intact and carried into the sea to sink and break apart in the surf. Two previous attempts to locate the plane's wreckage in the surrounding ocean, including a 2019 operation conducted by marine archaeologist Robert Ballard, famed for his discovery of the wreck of the Titanic, proved fruitless, Gillespie said. A plane-shaped sonar image from elsewhere on the sea floor turned out to be a pile of rocks. "I'd love to find that airplane. It ain't gonna happen," Gillespie said. Pettigrew and his team are betting otherwise. To them, the multi-branched shape first noticed in a 2020 satellite image resembles an aircraft fuselage and wings. They assert that the object, or part of it, has since been spotted in earlier aerial images of the island's lagoon dating as far back as 1938. Gillespie said he is certain that the object in question was actually a fallen pandanus tree, a palm-like evergreen native to the island region, that washed into the lagoon. "You can see the root ball. You can see the branches," Gillespie said in the interview. "It's a tree. People see what they want to see." 'GAS IS RUNNING LOW' The official US government view has long been that the Electra ran out of fuel and crashed at sea near its refueling destination of Howland Island, another dot of land about 400 miles northwest of Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island. Earhart was last seen taking off in her Electra on July 2, 1937, from Papua New Guinea en route to Gardner, about 2,500 miles (4,000 km) to the east, during a multi-stage attempt to become the first woman to pilot a plane around the world. Definitive radio contact with the plane was lost the next day after Earhart, 39, reported "gas is running low," followed by her final known transmission giving her geographical line of position. The disappearance spawned the largest US government search ever undertaken for a lost aircraft, including a flyover of Gardner, but no trace of the Electra or its crew was found at the time. The $900,000 Purdue mission, consisting of 17 people, plans to remain on Nikumaroro for five days before making the six-day return boat trip to the Kiribati capital, Tarawa, according to Schultz. Purdue, based in West Lafayette, Indiana, would ultimately seek to bring back any bits of the Lockheed Electra that might be recovered. Earhart was essentially a visiting faculty member at Purdue for two years as a women's career counselor and advisor to the school's aeronautics department. A Purdue research grant paid for development of the Electra, which she called her "flying laboratory." Purdue lawyer Schultz said if the plane were found, no artifacts would be removed from it on this trip. Any effort to extract the aircraft wreckage would require further permission from the Kiribati government, he said.

item.title: Mikko Rantanen, Stars ride momentum into matchup vs. Penguins
item.description: Mikko Rantanen looks to continue his strong start to the season when the Dallas Stars visit the Pittsburgh Penguins on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Mikko Rantanen looks to continue his strong start to the season when the Dallas Stars visit the Pittsburgh Penguins on Saturday. Rantanen has six points in his past three games, including four points in a 4-0 road win over the Buffalo Sabres on Thursday. The Penguins will be playing the second contest of a back-to-back set and looking to snap a three-game losing streak (0-2-1) following a 3-2 shootout loss to the host Columbus Blue Jackets on Friday. A goal from Pittsburgh's Evgeni Malkin early in the third period tied it 2-2 and forced overtime. The Penguins had that opportunity because backup goalie Sergei Murashov stopped 43 shots. "He was awesome. Just really steady and made some big saves for us," Pittsburgh captain Sidney Crosby said about Murashov. "There were some extended shifts there where they controlled a lot of the play. I thought that he allowed ourselves to get organized a bit." Malkin notched his third goal of the season, but Crosby has just two points (both assists) through five games. Bryan Rust has provided a spark and scored his second goal in two games back from injury for the Penguins, who opened the season by scoring 13 goals in two games but have totaled seven in their past three. "I mean, the guys battled back to get that point," Penguins coach Dan Muse said, "but at the same time, I feel like we just left too much of that game on the table. You're going to walk away, good to get the point, but you're disappointed in the overall game and what I know we're capable of." Rantanen had a goal and three assists on Thursday as Dallas beat Buffalo for its second straight win. It was Rantanen's 26th career game with at least four points. Dallas' Jason Robertson, Sam Steel and Roope Hintz also scored, and Wyatt Johnston had three assists. "I just like the game all of our guys are giving us right now," Stars coach Glen Gulutzan said. "Our 'D' has been moving the puck great the last couple games, and our forwards are working to spots for them, so we're a little connected. We've just got to keep stacking here. We've got to stack plays and games up on each other." If Jake Oettinger starts in goal Saturday night, he would be looking for his third straight shutout. He made 26 saves against the Sabres to follow up on 13-save effort in a 5-0 win against the San Jose Sharks on Monday. "I thought (Thursday) we were even better than the last game," Gulutzan said. "I thought we were good against a really good hockey team." It is the second time in his career that Oettinger has posted back-to-back shutouts. His shutout streak is at 146:55, the second longest of his career behind a 154:20 stretch from March 28-April 7, 2024. Oettinger is 7-1-0 with a 1.87 goals-against average and a .932 save percentage versus the Penguins in his career. Pittsburgh's likely starter, Arturs Silovs, has never faced the Stars. The Stars took both games against the Penguins last season. Rantanen scored the shootout winner in a 3-2 game at Dallas last December, and the Stars prevailed 6-3 at Pittsburgh in March. --Field Level Media

item.title: The midterm strategy driving Democrats deep into Trump country
item.description: It may seem like overreach, but Democrats say they want to force Republicans to spend money defending safe seats, draining resources from swing districts that will decide control of the House.
item.dc:creator: Leah Douglas, Joseph Ax, Tim Reid
item.content:encoded: On paper, Democrat Justin Pearson, a 31-year-old Tennessee state legislator, has little chance of winning the state's 9th Congressional District, which Republican lawmakers redrew months ago from a Democratic stronghold to a deeply Republican seat. Yet this week the national Democratic Party added the rural district to its list of midterm targets in November, part of a broader strategy to compete in President Donald Trump's conservative heartland despite long odds of flipping it. On its face, the strategy may look like Democratic overreach. Voters living in the 9th District's newly reconfigured boundaries, for instance, picked Trump by more than 21 points in 2024. More than a dozen Democratic operatives, strategists and candidates told Reuters the goal in part is to force Republicans to spend money defending safe seats, draining resources from the swing districts that will decide control of the US House. By expanding the map, the party is also signaling to donors that races are becoming more competitive amid high prices and the Iran war driving Trump's unpopularity, helping unlock money that might otherwise stay on the sidelines, they said. "These expansions force Republicans to go on defense in more districts," said one House campaign official, speaking on the condition of anonymity. "It's also a signal to donors and outside groups that House Democrats are taking these races seriously." REPUBLICANS DISMISSIVE OF NEW MAP The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the party's US House campaign arm, this week added Pearson's race and 13 others to its target list, expanding its battlefield to 66 Republican-held seats. Getting on the target list gives candidates access to national party staff and campaign tools, while also raising their profiles with donors, potentially opening new streams of fundraising for their campaigns. There are early signs the strategy is having some effect. Republican-aligned groups have begun spending in some newly added districts, while two Democratic campaigns in Republican districts told Reuters their fundraising accelerated after being placed on the target list. Republicans have dismissed the idea that Democrats have a serious chance of defeating their party in districts that overwhelmingly voted for Trump in 2024. Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee - the party's House campaign group - accused the Democratic Party of "stretching its map a mile wide and an inch deep, pretending every district in America is suddenly a battleground." He said the strategy will force Democrats to spend in long-shot contests when the party is already being outspent by Republicans. Analysts, too, are skeptical. "I'll take it seriously when they actually put their money where their mouth is. There is a point at which it becomes fantasy land," said David Wasserman, an elections analyst at the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, which rates many of these races as safely Republican. Democrats say they have chosen these districts for a number of reasons, including the quality of their candidates and the chance they might pull off upset wins to increase the size of a potential House majority. FOLLOWING THE MONEY It remains unclear how much money Democrats will ultimately devote to the newly added districts. Recent campaign finance filings are not yet available, and the party declined to tell Reuters where it is spending or how much it plans to spend on its expanded map. But there are signs Republicans are paying attention. Restoration of America PAC, funded primarily by billionaire Richard Uihlein, spent nearly $750,000 on digital ads backing Republican David Flippo in Nevada's 2nd District last week, according to Federal Election Commission filings. The district, which Trump carried by 14 points in 2024, is among the recent additions to the Democratic target list. "Democrats are on offense, Republicans are running scared, even in deep-red territory, and our expansive map reflects it," DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene said in a statement. The new target list includes districts in Arkansas, New York and Virginia that Trump carried by as many as 24 points. Democrats say rising costs and dissatisfaction with some Trump policies are creating openings in rural and Republican-leaning areas. "Rural America is unhappy with tariffs and rising fuel and farm costs, and that's pushing us into redder areas," Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said. Democrats will need a net gain of four to retake the House. However, only about 50 of the 435 House races are expected to be competitive. TENNESSEE DREAMING Tennessee Republicans in May split the heavily Democratic Memphis area into three districts, transforming the 9th from a majority-Black urban seat into a sprawling district stretching more than 200 miles (322 km) across rural western Tennessee, a change that made the seat significantly more favorable to Republicans. Yet Pearson says he has found independent and Republican voters frustrated by the high cost of living who are open to voting Democratic. "We've traveled across all 15 counties, filling churches and community centers in places people said we couldn't compete," said Pearson, a Black lawmaker who gained national attention in 2023 when the Republican-majority legislature expelled him for joining a gun-violence protest at the state Capitol. Republicans have portrayed Pearson as an outspoken progressive activist, pointing to his participation in gun-control and voting-rights protests. "The people in Tennessee Nine, they have a clear choice. They can choose confidence over chaos, and they can choose common sense over communism, and they can choose a lawmaker over a troublemaker," his Republican opponent, state senator Brent Taylor, told Reuters. There has been little public polling on the race, which Cook rates "Solid Republican." EXCITE DONORS Being added to the target list can quickly pay dividends for a campaign. Candidates or representatives from four Democratic campaigns on the DCCC's list told Reuters they either expected to see a boost in donations or were already seeing an uptick since their addition. Pearson said his campaign has seen a surge of financial support after being added to the list, which would boost his get-out-the-vote operation. "This race is going to be tight. It's going to be close. It's going to come down to how many people can we see before Election Day, knocking on those doors and reaching out to them directly," he said. But Democrats' ambitions are constrained by a relative cash shortage. While Democratic candidates nationally have outraised their Republican opponents, Republican national party committees and Republican-aligned super PACs have far outstripped Democratic counterparts in money raised. Democrats in tough races in the expanded map said they are connecting with small-dollar donors by focusing on cost-of-living issues and campaigning heavily at town halls and other local appearances.

item.title: The Week in Breakingviews: For whom the bell rings
item.description: As US stock markets set new records, this week’s update looks at some fresh cracks in the foundations of the artificial intelligence craze. Plus the threat to banks’ interest margins from AI agents, and Chinese car giant BYD’s attempt to follow Toyota’s global road.
item.dc:creator: Peter Thal Larsen
item.content:encoded: Welcome back! Governments across the West face rising bond yields. Will this trigger overdue tax reform and fiscal restraint, or a debt crisis? Let me know what you think. If this newsletter was forwarded to you, sign up here to get it in your inbox every weekend. OPENING LINE “Allison Kirkby is looking like Britain’s answer to Jamie Dimon. The BT (BT.L) CEO has just stepped in to buy up the carcass of indebted telecom group TalkTalk, just as the JPMorgan (JPM.N) boss is known for saving weak US banks.” Read more: [USN:L6N45R0MI TEXT:"BT’s vulture M&A dials up a worthwhile connection"] FIVE THINGS I LEARNED FROM BREAKINGVIEWS THIS WEEK Hiring a tanker to transit through the Strait of Hormuz to China now costs $1.2 million a day. ([USN:L6N45R0LH TEXT:"Tolls look more appealing"]) Discretionary government spending in Brazil accounts for less than 2% of GDP. ([USN:L6N45R0RL TEXT:"Little room for cuts"]) South Korea’s Samsung is set to make more profit than larger rival Nvidia this year. ([USN:L6N45U03L TEXT:"Valuations are very different"]) The price of jet fuel is double the average for last year. ([USN:L6N45L0U4 TEXT:"Trouble for engine specialists"]) Brewing giant AB InBev has launched a protein beer in Brazil. ([USN:L6N45R0VX TEXT:"But “proteinmaxxing” has limits"]) BURNING POINT When writing about financial markets, as when investing in them, timing is everything. By that yardstick, the cover story published by Barron’s in March 2000 can claim to be one of the best-timed works of financial journalism ever. Under the headline “ Burning Up ”, the article made the simple but devastating point that many hot internet startups of the era were using their financial resources so quickly they would run out of cash before the end of the year. It appeared 10 days after what turned out to be the peak of the dotcom bubble. Equity and debt markets dried up and valuations collapsed. It would be 15 years before the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite Index surpassed its previous peak. As the Nasdaq and S&P 500 benchmarks [USN:L6N45S0IV TEXT:"break records"] again this week, it is tempting to look at fresh cracks in the market’s foundations. There are plenty of contenders. Take Firmus Technologies, an Australian data centre operator backed by chip giant Nvidia (NVDA.O) and alternative asset manager Blackstone (BX.N) , which hoped to complete the country’s largest initial public offering in three decades. The so-called “neocloud” builds server farms and leases them to large tech companies. As Antony Currie [USN:L6N45S1EE TEXT:"explained"], executives touted a novel valuation measure – known as EV+1/EBIT+2 – to highlight its prospects. This unconventional ratio compares a company’s enterprise value – its market capitalisation plus net debt – in 12 months’ time to the earnings before interest and tax it expects to generate two years hence. The idea was to encourage investors to see hefty upfront investments in terms of their future payoff. It didn’t work. Firmus on Friday [USN:L6N45V00W TEXT:"cancelled its $31 billion listing"] citing “recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions.” Or take the news, reported by the Financial Times on Thursday, that OpenAI’s revenue was running at an annualised rate of about $50 billion in September – $20 billion less than the figure the FT and others had previously reported. The revelation is mainly a reminder that multiplying a company’s monthly revenue by 12 is a [USN:L6N3ZY167 TEXT:"crude and unreliable"] way of gauging its financial health. Nevertheless, it prompted an across-the-board selloff in listed tech stocks. These setbacks will not, on their own, prick the artificial intelligence bubble. Other data centre operators are making healthy returns on their investments in chips and energy: as Rob Cyran [USN:L6N45T0Y8 TEXT:"points out"], SpaceX’s (SPCX.O) chief financial officer says Elon Musk’s company should earn back its initial outlay in less than a year. Meanwhile, OpenAI’s mooted trillion-dollar-plus valuation depends less on how much revenue it brought in last month than what it might be generating in two or three years’ time. Shareholders also have a habit of freaking out prematurely. Recall the brief selloff triggered by the release of Chinese startup DeepSeek’s new AI model in early 2025. Still, investors are increasingly jittery. The yield on 10-year US government debt – the main reference point for global borrowing costs – has risen by around a percentage point since late April, changing the calculus for debt-heavy projects. Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO, which is supposed to take place before the end of November , will be a [USN:L6N45F0XJ TEXT:"test of confidence"]. Only with hindsight, though, will we be able to point to the article that marked the top of the current frenzy. CHART OF THE WEEK When code-writing artificial intelligence bots tanked software stocks, investors dubbed it the SaaSpocalypse. Now banks are in the firing line. The arrival of digital assistants like Meta Platforms’ (META.O) Muse could help complacent consumers earn higher interest rates on deposits, squeezing the net interest margin (NIM) banks make on the spread with loan charges. Stephen Gandel [USN:L6N45N19E TEXT:"crunched the numbers"] on the $3.8 trillion currently stashed in US savings accounts. Raising the rate from the current 1.9% to 4% would cost those lenders a hefty $79 billion a year in lost income. Get ready for the NIMageddon. THE WEEK IN PODCASTS The revelation that Manchester City benefited from sham contracts worth $1.1 billion over almost a decade has roiled English soccer. It also has far-reaching business and financial implications (See [USN:L6N45O0WL TEXT:"Britain’s soccer sham"]). Liam Proud and Jon Sindreu joined Jonathan Guilford in the Viewsroom to debate whether it’s possible to design a level playing field when the financial stakes are so high, and what the scandal means for investors rushing to buy big sports teams. The notion that stocks and bonds follow a rational path has been widely debunked. But are idiosyncrasies becoming more visible? On The Big View I talked to Alex Edmans, the academic and author of “The Madness of Markets”, about whether the rules of investing have changed. PARTING SHOT Toyota rose from being a Japanese upstart to become the world’s largest carmaker. So it’s tempting to imagine whether BYD, the Chinese electric vehicle juggernaut, can follow the same route. Indeed, founder Wang Chuanfu says he aims to become the biggest manufacturer of automobiles on the planet by 2030, which would mean overtaking Toyota. Yet as Katrina Hamlin [USN:L6N45K0H1 TEXT:"writes"], the road for BYD is a lot bumpier and narrower than the one followed by its Japanese rival. The Chinese company must overcome stagnating sales, export barriers, hostile governments overseas, and cut-throat competition at home. Toyota has shown the way, but BYD will have to drive even faster to match it. Want to receive The Week in Breakingviews in your inbox every Saturday? Sign up for the newsletter here . item.title: Hastings like a local
item.description: Our desk editor’s guide to castle views, shipwrecks and seasonal festivals.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Hudson
item.content:encoded: REUTERS/Illustration/Kate Evans Famous for the eponymous battle of 1066 that inspired the Bayeux Tapestry , the British seaside town of Hastings — my home of the last decade — has a thriving cultural life, magnificent natural setting and rough-around-the-edges charm that grows on you quickly. The beach is the star attraction, atmospheric pubs and cafes abound, and of course there are Hastings' evocative historical sites — not least the ruined Hastings Castle , constructed by William, Duke of Normandy, after winning the English throne. I grew up in Brighton, also on the country's southern coast, and settled in Hastings with my family after postings in Berlin, Amsterdam, and Istanbul for Reuters. The sea air and screeching seagulls made it quickly feel like home. Hastings is not immune to the problems affecting Britain's coastal towns, including a lack of employment and some deprivation, and it has seen its fortunes rise and fall over the decades. But the town is drawing more visitors and blossoming with fresh energy and new ventures. Here is how to visit Hastings like a local: Getting around: Hastings and neighbouring St Leonards-on-Sea, once a Regency-era resort and now the edgier of the two, form one urban area that is best explored on foot. Walking from central St Leonards to Hastings along the seafront promenade takes less than one hour. The elegant apartment blocks give way to British seaside staples like mini golf, go-karts and amusement arcades before you reach the Old Town, with its compact streets of timbered houses. People relax at Goat Ledge beach cafe at St Leonards-on-Sea, next to Hastings, Britain, October 4, 2026. Hastings has one of the largest working beach-launched fishing fleets in Europe. REUTERS/Toby Melville A person fishes off the harbour wall in Hastings Old Town. REUTERS/Toby Melville People walk on Hastings Pier, styled on the deck of an ocean liner. REUTERS/Toby Melville Hastings Old Town, Hastings Pier and Hastings beach are viewed from East Hill. REUTERS/Toby Melville If arriving by train, alight at St Leonards Warrior Square station and walk down Kings Road, a vibrant street of cafes, second-hand bookshops, vintage furniture stores and artist-run outlets selling bold screenprints and ceramics. It holds a street market on the first Saturday of each month, featuring handicrafts, organic food, and jewellery. Turn left at the end of the road for your first glimpse of the sea. What to see: One of my favourite spots on the beach is the strip along Warrior Square and Bottle Alley, a split-level promenade. Beachfront cafes such as Goat Ledge , Starsky & Hatch and The Selkie have breathed new life into this area, and it is a popular place to bask in the sun with a coffee or lunch. The brightly painted wooden huts, twinkly lights and bistro tables on the pebbles bring a festival vibe and you’ll often hear live music here. A short walk further along the seafront brings you to George Street, a charming pedestrian lane of restaurants, pubs and gift shops at the foot of the castle. The West Hill lift is a historic Victorian funicular railway that will transport you up to the Norman castle for £5.50 ($7.40) round-trip. There you’ll find magnificent views across the English Channel towards France, as well as yoga classes and outdoor film screenings. The West Hill is also home to the Smugglers Adventure , a fun attraction that tells stories of piracy and smuggling in a warren of caves reputedly once used to conceal contraband. In the 1960s, the caves housed a subterranean nightclub. To return to the Old Town, hop back on the funicular or follow one of the several steep, winding paths. Look out for the twittens — narrow, medieval alleyways between the houses, as you weave through All Saints Street, Tackleway and the High Street. What to eat: If you fancy seafood, the grilled “catch of the day” fish bap (or sandwich) at Goat Ledge is always delicious. Alternatively, pick up traditional fish and chips and eat them on the beach. Just watch out for diving seagulls going for your chips. People relax at Goat Ledge beach cafe at St Leonards-on-Sea. REUTERS/Toby Melville People relax at Selkie Seafood Bar at St Leonards-on-Sea. REUTERS/Toby Melville Oyster shells and other sea food are seen on a beachside table at Selkie Seafood Bar at St Leonards-on-Sea. REUTERS/Toby Melville In St Leonards, Half Man! Half Burger! has some of the best burgers — meat and vegetarian — I've ever tasted, and Three Faces has incredible tapas. Culture fix: Hastings is unusual in having a beach-launched fishing fleet, with the boats hauled back on to the pebbles when not in use. Right beside them is Hastings Contemporary , a wonderful art gallery whose design mirrors that of the historic black Net Shops used for stowing fishing equipment. A fisherman throws equipment from a boat after returning from a fishing trip in The Stade area of Hastings Old Town. Hastings has one of the largest working beach-launched fishing fleets in Europe. REUTERS/Toby Melville A tractor pulls a fishing boat up the beach in The Stade area of Hastings Old Town. REUTERS/Toby Melville Walk along Rock-a-Nore Road and stop at the excellent (and free) Fishermen's Museum , which highlights the history of the fleet and tragic storms that have struck. Opposite is the 1902 East Hill lift, Britain's steepest funicular, which takes you up to Hastings Country Park — a beautiful expanse of rolling sandstone cliffs, with breathtaking views down to the sea. Look out for the roaming ponies that graze the heathland. A young person views exhibits at the Fishermen's Museum in Hastings Old Town. REUTERS/Toby Melville For music lovers, Hastings Philharmonic runs excellent classical concerts throughout the year. Check the tides: Hastings has a pebble beach, but at low tide, vast stretches of sand are exposed, offering ample space for long strolls. I like to time sea swims for high tide and beach walks for low tide. If this falls at sunset, you'll find the beach packed with locals savouring the views. Look out for hagstones, pebbles with natural holes. A few times a year, when the tide falls below 60 cm (2 feet), you can glimpse the wreck of the Amsterdam, a Dutch East India Company ship that ran aground in 1749 outside St Leonards and was exposed by shifting sands in 1969. It makes for an eerie sight. A replica is moored outside Amsterdam's Maritime Museum , while Hastings' excellent Shipwreck Museum displays the bottles, spoons and other goods found onboard. The 1066 battlefield: A 15-minute train ride 6 miles (9.5 km) inland brings you to the town of Battle, where King Harold’s Saxon army was defeated by William’s Norman invaders. You can visit the former battlefield and ruined abbey, built by William's son on the spot where Harold perished, and explore a medieval gatehouse. Centuries on, walking the trail around the battlefield where thousands died remains a sombre and moving experience. A good pint: Hastings has no shortage of charming local boozers. The 16th-century Stag Inn on All Saints Street has a pretty, tiered garden overlooking the rooftops. Look out for the mummified cat that was found encased within the chimney — a practice said to ward off evil in British folklore. Another good pub is the FILO (First In Last Out) on the High Street, with an unusual indoor fire pit and cosy wooden booths that are always packed on weekends.
