It brews its own traditional ales and has been joined in recent years by other craft beer makers, including The Brewing Brothers , who run three excellent venues. In the Old Town, the Jenny Lind , named after a 19th-century Swedish opera singer, is one of Hastings' most-loved pubs with regular acoustic nights and folk, rock and sea shanty sessions. Over in St Leonards, The Piper draws a younger crowd and holds regular gigs upstairs. Get festive: Dig out green clothes and flower crowns for the annual "Jack in the Green" folk festival on the first Monday of May. Dancers and drummers dressed in green parade through the town and up on to the West Hill, where the Jack — a crowned figure clad in foliage — is symbolically slain to release the spirit of summer. It's all rather reminiscent of the 1973 folk horror film "The Wicker Man," and seems to get bigger every year. A participant attends the annual May Day bank holiday Jack In The Green parade and festival. REUTERS/Toby Melville Participants attend the annual May Day bank holiday Jack In The Green parade and festival. REUTERS/Toby Melville A participant attends the annual May Day bank holiday Jack In The Green parade and festival. REUTERS/Toby Melville In July, locals rustle up striped shirts and eye patches for Pirate Weekend , which brings three days of live music to the shore, and a noisy parade through the town for all “pirates” to join. In October, an annual bonfire marks the anniversary of the Norman Conquest, with a flaming torch procession through the Old Town and a huge blaze and fireworks on the beach. CITY MEMO DATA POINTS Population: 91,000 Price of a cup of coffee: £3.80 ($5) for a flat white at Starsky & Hatch Price of an ice cream: £3.00 ($4) for a Flake 99 — vanilla soft-serve served in a wafer cone with a small chocolate bar on top — from Dom's Ices . For £3.90 ($5.17), you can get a scoop of gelato at Di Pola's . Great place to see a sunset: The coastal paths of the Country Park, or the West or East Hill

item.title: Renshaw leads Australian resistance with unbeaten hundred
item.description: Australia’s Matt Renshaw scored an unbeaten century to keep up his side’s resistance as they went to lunch 277-8 on the second day of the first test against South Africa at Kingsmead on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gleeson
item.content:encoded: Australia’s Matt Renshaw scored an unbeaten century to keep up his side’s resistance as they went to lunch 277-8 on the second day of the first test against South Africa at Kingsmead on Saturday. The touring side had been in a precarious position at 124-6 on the opening day but Renshaw led a fightback before bad light stopped play on Friday and continued his form into the second morning, reaching his second test ton almost a decade after his first against Pakistan in Sydney in 2017. The 30-year-old brought up his century off 204 balls with his 10th four and was 102 not out at lunch, alongside Nathan Lyon on seven. Renshaw, who was expected to open the batting but surprisingly dropped down the order to No. 5, was 46 not out overnight and moved to his half century with a boundary off the second ball of the day. Renshaw shared an 86-run partnership with captain Pat Cummins, before the skipper got a thick edge to Wiaan Mulder and was caught at second slip by Aiden Markram for 43. Mulder bowled Mitchell Starc for six but by then Australia had added a healthy 43 runs to their overnight total of 187-6 as the pitch looked to have lost the bounce and movement of the first day. Mulder was the pick of the home bowlers with figures of 4-51 off 22 overs and could complete his first test five-wicket haul after lunch.

item.title: Rosatom says it wins tribunal ruling in Finnish nuclear plant dispute
item.description: Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom said on Saturday that an International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) tribunal had ruled in its favour in a long-running dispute with Finnish utility Fennovoima over the cancelled Hanhikivi-1 nuclear power project.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom said on Saturday that an International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) tribunal had ruled in its favour in a long-running dispute with Finnish utility Fennovoima over the cancelled Hanhikivi-1 nuclear power project. Rosatom said the tribunal found that Fennovoima had unlawfully terminated the contract for the construction of the planned plant in northern Finland in 2022. The parties have been locked in legal disputes since Fennovoima scrapped the 7-billion-euro ($7.8 billion) project in May 2022, citing significant delays and political risks shortly after Russia launched its conflict in Ukraine. Rosatom said the tribunal found that the project was making good progress when it was terminated. "Today's victory is important, but not final. We will continue to prove that we are right regarding the Finnish project in courts of various instances," Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev said in a statement. Fennovoima did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The contract to build the 1.2 gigawatt plant was signed in 2013 with Fennovoima, a consortium in which Finnish stakeholders including Fortum, Outokumpu and SSAB originally controlled two thirds through a joint venture, and the Russian side held one third. After the project's termination, Fennovoima wound down its operations and is primarily engaged in legal proceedings. ($1 = 0.8928 euros)

item.title: Singapore sprint underway after rain delay
item.description: The start of the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race on Saturday was delayed by half an hour due to heavy rain at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.
item.dc:creator: Rohith Nair
item.content:encoded: The start of the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race on Saturday was delayed by half an hour due to heavy rain at the Marina Bay Street Circuit. A shower minutes before the scheduled 5 p.m. (0900 GMT) start sent fans and officials rushing for cover while standing water around turns 2 and 3 forced the FIA to put back the start after the medical car had assessed track conditions. Once the standing water was cleared, the FIA said drivers would do two formation laps behind the safety car as teams quickly swapped out the slick tyres for intermediates. "The spray is very bad," McLaren's Oscar Piastri said on the team radio as the drivers did two formation laps before a standing start for the final sprint race of the season. Red Bull's Max Verstappen took [USN:L1N45V0HG TEXT:"pole position for the sprint"] ahead of Mercedes driver George Russell and Ferrari's Charles Leclerc. Last weekend, the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia descended into chaos as heavy rain at the Sepang circuit triggered [USN:L1N45Q01D TEXT:"multiple delays and a suspended start procedure"] that left drivers scrambling in treacherous conditions.

item.title: Thailand prepares to host IMF-World Bank meetings
item.description: Thailand is preparing to host the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok from October 12–18, bringing together more than 15,000 participants from 191 countries, including central bank governors, economic policymakers and business leaders, for discussions on the world economy.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Thailand is preparing to host the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok from October 12–18, bringing together more than 15,000 participants from 191 countries, including central bank governors, economic policymakers and business leaders, for discussions on the world economy. To ease traffic, Bangkok government offices will work from home on October 12, 14 and 15, while October 13 is an existing public holiday and October 16 has been declared a special government and bank holiday, with private companies and state enterprises asked to consider suitable arrangements. Security has been tightened at the meeting venue in central Bangkok and 21 official hotels, according to the authorities. About 500 Tourist Police officers will also help secure the venue, delegate hotels and tourist attractions through undercover deployments, patrols, drones and motorcade escorts coordinated with around 39 embassies, Tourist Police Bureau Commissioner Phongsiam Meekhanthong said. Visiting leaders include Swiss President Guy Parmelin, making the first official visit to Thailand by a Swiss president in 22 years, and Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, the Thai Foreign Ministry said. Participants’ spending could generate 1.05–2.25 billion baht for the Thai economy, according to the Thai Finance Ministry. More than 320 electric vehicles will serve participants to cut carbon emissions, the Thai Finance Ministry said. Heavy to very heavy rain is forecast for Bangkok and surrounding provinces on October 10–11, potentially causing localised flooding, the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration warned. This comes after parts of the city [USN:L6N45I012 TEXT:"flooded"] two weeks ago following 320 mm (12.6 inches) of rain over three days.

item.title: All Blacks crush Australia with second-half blitz to retain Bledisloe Cup
item.description: Australia's hopes of wresting back the Bledisloe Cup for the first time in a generation were crushed in familiar fashion in a comprehensive 50-19 loss to New Zealand at Auckland's Eden Park on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Australia's hopes of wresting back the Bledisloe Cup for the first time in a generation were crushed in familiar fashion in a comprehensive 50-19 loss to New Zealand at Auckland's Eden Park on Saturday. The Wallabies were in touch at 17-14 down at halftime but the All Blacks scored five tries after the break to ensure they will retain the symbol of trans-Tasman Sea supremacy for a 24th straight year ahead of next week's second test in Sydney. Tries from Peter Lakai, Tupou Vaa'i, Cam Roigard, skipper Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby and Will Jordan combined with 15 points from the boot of flyhalf Damian McKenzie got the All Blacks back to winning ways after three straight losses to South Africa. "We were hurting a little bit after the (South Africa series), but it's awesome to come home, play in front of our fans, our people. We've missed it, and to get a result like that, it's hugely proud of the boys," said Taylor, whose try helped New Zealand extend their unbeaten run at Eden Park to 54 matches since 1994. "This is home for us ... You see ex-All Blacks standing on the sidelines. You want to do it for those men, the people that have been before you, and you just want to continue the legacy." Australia, who came into the game unbeaten in six matches and looking for a first win at Eden Park since 1986, scored first-half tries through fullback Tom Wright and captain Harry Wilson and earned a late consolation score from hooker Josh Nasser. “Playing them here, it's always going to be tough and we did a really good job to be in the fight after that first half,” said Wilson. “We fought back really well and then we had an opportunity at the start of the second half and we blew it, and then it was tough to get the ball back for the next 30 minutes.” The Wallabies, buoyed by a win over world champions South Africa last month, dominated the opening exchanges and got their reward in the eighth minute when fullback Wright cleverly straightened up an attacking move to score the opening try. The aerial battle was always going to be a key factor and New Zealand were enjoying the better of it with Jordie Barrett winning one duel and feeding McKenzie, who scythed through the defence before feeding flanker Lakai to level up the scores. The All Blacks were also getting a width in the attack that was causing Australia problems and the home side cashed in to take a 14-7 lead in the 16th minute, when Vaa'i barrelled low and hard through the defence at the end of a multi-phase attack. Ryan Lonergan missed a kickable penalty for Australia in the 24th minute, but McKenzie made no mistake from closer range nine minutes later to extend the lead to 10 points. The five minutes before halftime is traditionally a fruitful stage of the game for New Zealand, but it was Australia who scored three minutes before the break, with Ben Donaldson scooting through a gap in the defence and finding Wilson in support. Australia again came firing out of the blocks in the second half but New Zealand earned the first points after 50 minutes when scrumhalf Roigard darted over the line off the back of a rolling maul to extend their lead to 24-14. The All Blacks were now relentless in attack and hooker Taylor, captaining the side for the second time, scored their fourth try five minutes later. The Wallabies were now struggling to hold onto the ball and wingers Carter, Moorby and Jordan capitalised on the remorseless pressure from the All Blacks in the last quarter to put the game well beyond the visitors.

item.title: Struggling Canadiens face Red Wings after three straight losses
item.description: The Montreal Canadiens have lost three straight (0-2-1) going into their game against the visiting Detroit Red Wings in an Original Six matchup Saturday night.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The Montreal Canadiens have lost three straight (0-2-1) going into their game against the visiting Detroit Red Wings in an Original Six matchup Saturday night. The Habs' last two defeats came at home, the most recent a 5-2 loss to the Nashville Predators on Thursday night. The Canadiens fell despite being the better team and out-chancing the Predators for most of the contest. Montreal had a 33-20 shot advantage. "I thought we outplayed them the majority of the game," said Canadiens captain Nick Suzuki, who picked up a goal. "We just didn't score on our chances." Montreal led 2-0 in the second period before surrendering five consecutive goals. Nashville tied it 2-2 on a power play with 32 seconds left in the middle period. "I thought we were playing a good game," Montreal goalie Jacob Fowler said. "The second period we were all over them and their goalie made some big saves there, and it sucks to give up that one late." A power-play goal by Nashville's Ryan O'Reilly with 3:16 left broke the 2-2 tie, and the Predators added two empty-net goals. Montreal coach Martin St. Louis juggled all but the third line of Phillip Danault between Zackary Bolduc and Alexandre Texier throughout the game. Alex Newhook also scored for the Canadiens. Fowler made 15 saves after he was recalled from AHL Laval on Wednesday in response to Sam Montembeault sustaining a lower-body injury in practice. Montembeault will be out 10 to 14 days. "We play like that, we'll probably win more than most," Canadiens forward Cole Caufield said. "... I feel pretty good going into Saturday." Suzuki has three goals and four assists through four games. The Red Wings, who have lost three of four this season, are also coming off a defeat in which they outshot their opponents by a wide margin. Detroit dropped a 6-3 decision to the visiting Seattle Kraken on Friday night, even though the Red Wings registered a 40-24 shot advantage. The Red Wings took a 2-1 lead four minutes into the second period on rookie defenseman William Wallinder's first career goal. However, the Kraken re-tied it just 39 seconds later, which began an onslaught of four goals in 9:26. "We got loose and impatient and didn't stick with it," Detroit coach Todd McLellan said. "And all of a sudden, the puck's in our net and we're chasing." Detroit starting goalie John Gibson was pulled after allowing five goals on 15 shots. He was replaced by Daniil Tarasov, who is scheduled to get his first Red Wings start Saturday night. The 27-year-old Russian gave up one goal on nine shots. Red Wings rookie Michael Brandsegg-Nygard got his first NHL goal in the third period after logging a second-period assist. Alex DeBrincat, playing in his 700th game, picked up his 600th career point by assisting on Wallinder's goal. "I just think we got a little lazy, a little soft on pucks," DeBrincat said. "... Learn from it, go on (Saturday) and get two points." Viktor Arvidsson also scored for Detroit, his team-leading third goal, all on the power play. The Red Wings won the last two of the three games between the teams last season, including a 4-0 victory in the lone meeting at Montreal. --Field Level Media

item.title: From 'cockroach' post to protest leader: India's Dipke tests Modi government
item.description: His six-word reply to the Supreme Court's chief justice shot him to fame.
item.dc:creator: Tora Agarwala
item.content:encoded: Indian police detained on Saturday Abhijeet Dipke, the political strategist who turned a "cockroach" jibe at unemployed youth into a nationwide protest movement that helped force the resignation of a federal minister. Police met Dipke's aircraft as it landed in the capital of New Delhi ahead of a rally demanding the resignation of the election chief over accusations of [USN:L4N45K0E7 TEXT:"voter list manipulation"] that critics say dropped about 130 million voters from a draft roll. "I have come to be arrested, arrest me ... I am not afraid of you guys," Dipke told police officers aboard the aircraft, in television images that showed one of them assuring him he was not being arrested, but rather that his cooperation was sought. Dipke, 31, born in a Dalit family on the lower rungs of India's caste system, shot to fame this year after his six-word response to Supreme Court Chief Justice Surya Kant's remarks likening unemployed youth to "cockroaches" went viral online. The post spawned the satirical "Cockroach Janta Party", an online movement that rapidly evolved into a political force. It mobilised mass street protests that culminated in the July resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan, a rare exit from Prime Minister Narendra Modi's cabinet, following sustained public pressure. Dipke's detention came after he called for a [USN:L1N45W00K TEXT:"fresh protest"] on Saturday seeking the resignation of election commission chief [USN:L4N45K0DB TEXT:"Gyanesh Kumar"] over the changes. The election panel says the figure, which is larger than the population of Japan, comprises entries flagged during draft revision, and that voters wrongly removed can enroll again. Bearded and usually wearing T-shirt and jeans, Dipke had led a protest in the southern tech hub of Bengaluru before travelling via Mumbai to the capital, where police detained him with two senior group leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. Despite a police crackdown in Delhi and tight protest restrictions, Dipke urged supporters to demonstrate peacefully, citing the example of Mahatma Gandhi, India's apostle of non-violence. "I don't know what will happen tomorrow," Dipke said in a video recorded before Saturday's flight. "But one thing I am sure of is that I am not going to be afraid. Neither am I going to step back. We have to save our democracy." Authorities called in thousands of security forces to fortify Delhi, with travel and telecoms links suspended, in a [USN:L1N45W00K TEXT:"lockdown"] designed to stop the youth protest. "Why is the prime minister so scared of the country's youth, the country's people?" Dipke asked before his flight. UNLIKELY EVENTS SET OFF BY SIX-WORD POST "What if all cockroaches come together?" was Dipke's question in a May social media post that almost overnight turned the political communications professional into one of the most recognisable faces of India's youth protest movement. He returned to India after completing a master's degree in public relations in the United States, saying his viral success had given him "a chance to do actual, meaningful work", despite threats he and his family received. The "Cockroach Janta Party" amassed millions of followers online and helped drive protests over leaks of a medical entrance examination paper affecting about 2 million candidates. The movement eventually focused its anger on Pradhan, who resigned on July 25. Since then, Dipke and his supporters, who see the group as a political pressure movement rather than a party, have campaigned on issues ranging from government school infrastructure to jobs for young people. It returned to the streets after a report last month in the Indian Express newspaper. The paper said two of election chief Kumar's deputies had repeatedly raised concerns about voter-roll revisions, registration procedures and the commission's digital systems. The poll body has said differing views are normal during internal deliberations. (This story has been corrected to fix the spelling of Abhijeet Dipke's first name in paragraph 1.)

item.title: Marquez takes championship lead with Indonesian GP sprint win
item.description: Ducati's Marc Marquez seized the lead in the championship standings for the first time in 2026 on Saturday by winning a dramatic Indonesian MotoGP sprint, after title rival Jorge Martin's race unravelled amid tyre issues.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ducati's Marc Marquez seized the lead in the championship standings for the first time in 2026 on Saturday by winning a dramatic Indonesian MotoGP sprint, after title rival Jorge Martin's race unravelled amid tyre issues. Marquez's eighth sprint victory of the campaign moved him to 343 points, four ahead of Martin, completing a remarkable comeback for the defending champion, who trailed then-series leader Marco Bezzecchi by 102 points after the Italian Grand Prix in May. "It was a very tough race, especially from the beginning, and then when I saw that Martin was leading, I pushed with all I have," said Marquez, who was left exhausted by the hot and humid conditions. In a chaotic start to the sprint, [USN:L4N45W00O TEXT:"polesitter Raul Fernandez"] and Bezzecchi found themselves lying in the gravel after the first turn, while Aprilia's Martin surged into the lead from the second row, with Marquez hot on his heels. Martin quickly stretched his advantage and appeared headed for victory before deliberately conceding the lead to Marquez with five laps remaining to avoid a tyre-pressure penalty. The 2024 MotoGP champion did his best to retake the lead from Marquez, but ran wide in his dogged pursuit and ultimately failed to finish on the podium, coming in fourth. Trackhouse rider Ai Ogura was second, with Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Racing) taking a third-placed finish on his birthday. "I did a big mistake on the third lap, fourth lap, and then he opened a gap," Marquez said. "In the last part of the race, I was able to catch him, I think he had some problem with the tyre pressure. "In the end, I felt better and better with the laps, my pace was better, but in the end, as always, I tried to manage the risk. These 12 points in the Mandalika sprint race are super important." The victory also appeared to end Marquez's run of misfortune in Indonesia. The Spaniard has endured a torrid record at Mandalika and suffered a season-ending collarbone injury there last year. On Sunday, the 33-year-old will be hoping to complete his first-ever full MotoGP race at the Mandalika circuit after a string of crashes and technical setbacks in previous appearances.

item.title: Voile-Barrier, première femme en solitaire sur un géant des mers
item.description: Alexia Barrier paraît toute petite à la barre d'Idec Sport-CIC, un trimaran de 32 mètres capable de filer à plus de 40 nœuds. Bientôt, elle sera seule à bord.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Daheron
item.content:encoded: Alexia Barrier paraît toute petite à la barre d'Idec Sport-CIC, un trimaran de 32 mètres capable de filer à plus de 40 nœuds. Bientôt, elle sera seule à bord. Le 1er novembre, la skippeuse française de 46 ans embarquera à Saint-Malo sur ce géant des mers pour tenter ce qu'aucune femme n'a encore fait : naviguer en solitaire en Ultim sur la Route du Rhum. "C'est la plus grosse machine engagée en course au large dans le monde", a-t-elle expliqué à Reuters. "Il n'en existe que huit sur la planète. Donc je suis heureuse, fière et privilégiée d'en être la skippeuse." Par une lumineuse matinée d'octobre, Alexia Barrier sort dans la rade de Brest son immense trimaran rouge, 23 mètres de large, surmonté d'un mât qui culmine à 34 mètres au-dessus de la mer. Elle hisse la grand-voile au rythme de "Meet Me Halfway" des Black Eyed Peas, répétant les manœuvres qu'elle devra bientôt effectuer seule. Même dans une brise légère, le bateau accélère rapidement jusqu'à 23 nœuds. "Les voiles sont énormes. C'est vraiment puissant. Une voile pèse plus de 100 kilos. J'en pèse 55", relève-t-elle. "Ça va tellement vite que si vous faites une erreur, ça peut très mal finir, parce que vous pouvez abîmer le bateau et vous blesser. Je suis super heureuse, mais je n'ai jamais été aussi concentrée." Le trimaran a déjà vogué sur l'eau à près de 46 nœuds, son record. Ce jour-là, ce n'était pas la Niçoise qui tenait la barre. "C'était un sans-cerveau", rigole-t-elle. "UNE ÉVIDENCE" Il y a neuf mois, Alexia Barrier a établi avec sept équipières le premier temps de référence d'un équipage 100% féminin sur le Trophée Jules-Verne, un tour du monde sans escale et sans assistance en multicoque. Dans quelques semaines, elle devra troquer cette camaraderie pour la solitude si particulière de la course au large en solitaire. "En rentrant du Trophée Jules-Verne, c'était une évidence", dit-elle à propos de sa décision de s'aligner sur la Route du Rhum. "J'ai l'impression que c'était une autre vie. Quand je navigue en solitaire, mes équipières me manquent. Parfois, je me surprends à chercher l'une d'entre elles à son poste habituel et elle n'est pas là." La Française peaufine encore la playlist qui l'accompagnera pendant environ une semaine en mer. La musique sera l'une de ses rares compagnes à bord, tandis que son labrador restera à la maison. Mais il y aura peu de place pour la distraction à bord d'une machine aussi puissante, rapide et exigeante physiquement. Alexia Barrier sait aussi que ce voyage dépasse largement le simple enjeu du résultat sportif. Elle a pris l'habitude d'ouvrir les portes longtemps restées fermées aux femmes après avoir été l'une des 13 navigatrices à boucler le Vendée Globe et, donc, d'avoir dirigé le premier équipage 100% féminin à terminer le Trophée Jules-Verne. "OUVRIR UNE VOIE" "Ça fait partie de ma carrière. Je fais de la course au large depuis 20 ans maintenant, c'est ma vie. Pour moi, c'est une nouvelle étape", résume-t-elle. "D'une certaine façon, c'est cool d'être la première. Je peux ouvrir une voie pour d'autres femmes, ou des petites filles qui se demandent encore : 'Est-ce que j'essaie, est-ce que je me lance ?'" Afin d'intégrer la classe Ultim, "l'élite de la voile" créée en 2018, Alexia Barrier a dû non seulement engranger de l'expérience mais aussi réunir les financements et l'équipe nécessaires pour porter un tel projet. Encore aujourd'hui, elle peine à y croire. "J'ai rêvé trop grand", sourit-elle sur le pont du port du Moulin Blanc, à Brest. Ce rêve est devenu réalité et, à l'approche du départ, Alexia Barrier rêve encore un peu plus grand quand on lui parle de son objectif. "Dans mes rêves, si la magie opère, accéder au podium serait incroyable", confie-t-elle. "C'est important de se donner le droit de rêver grand." Personne ne le sait mieux qu'Alexia Barrier.

item.title: Barrier ready to make history in Route du Rhum on ocean-racing giant
item.description: Alexia Barrier looks impossibly small at the helm of IDEC Sport-CIC, a 32-metre (105-foot) trimaran capable of hurtling across the ocean at more than 40 knots. Soon, she will be entirely alone.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Daheron
item.content:encoded: Alexia Barrier looks impossibly small at the helm of IDEC Sport-CIC, a 32-metre (105-foot) trimaran capable of hurtling across the ocean at more than 40 knots. Soon, she will be entirely alone. On November 1, the 46-year-old French sailor will climb aboard the giant vessel in Saint-Malo and attempt something no woman has done before: race solo in the giant ULTIM class in the Route du Rhum. “It’s the biggest machine participating in offshore sailing around the world,” Barrier told Reuters. “Only eight of this kind are on the planet. So I’m happy, proud and privileged to be skipper of this machine.” On a bright October morning in Brest, Barrier looked tiny on the deck of the huge red trimaran, 23 metres (75 feet) wide with a mast towering 34 metres (112 feet) above the water. She hoisted the mainsail to the sound of the Black Eyed Peas’ “Meet Me Halfway”, rehearsing the manoeuvres she will soon have to perform entirely alone. Even in the light breeze, the boat quickly accelerated towards 23 knots. “The sails are huge. It’s really powerful. A sail is more than 100 kilos. I’m 55 kilos,” she said. “It goes so fast and if you make a mistake, it can be terrible because you can hurt the boat and hurt yourself. I’m super happy, but I’m more focused than ever.” The boat has reached speeds of around 46 knots. Barrier laughs about the prospect of matching that herself. “The record is about 46 knots, but you have to be a bit crazy to be at the helm at that speed,” she joked. FIRST ALL-FEMALE CREW Nine months ago, Barrier was leading the first all-female crew to set a reference time for the Jules Verne Trophy, sailing non-stop around the world. Now she is swapping that camaraderie for the peculiar solitude of single-handed ocean racing. “When I came back from the Jules Verne Trophy, for me it was obvious,” she said of taking on the Route du Rhum alone. “It feels like it was in another life when I’m sailing solo. I miss my crewmates. Sometimes I catch myself looking around, searching for one of them at her usual station and she’s not there.” Music will be one companion. Barrier is still working on the playlist that will soundtrack roughly a week alone at sea. But there will be little time for distraction aboard a machine where the combination of enormous power, speed and physical demands means a small error can quickly become a serious one. Barrier knows, too, that this voyage is about more than a finishing position. One of only 13 women to have completed the Vendee Globe, and now the skipper who led the all-female Jules Verne attempt, she has become accustomed to being the first woman through doors that have traditionally been difficult to open. “It’s part of my career. I’ve been racing for 20 years now, and it’s my life. For me, it’s a new step,” she said. “In a way, it’s cool to be the first. I can open a path for other women or little girls that are still wondering: ‘Shall I try, shall I do it?’” 'ELITE OF SAILING' Breaking into ULTIM racing required Barrier to find not only the experience but the money and team needed to operate at what she calls “the elite of sailing”. Even now she can scarcely believe where that journey has taken her. Standing on the dock in Brest, Barrier recalled thinking of the challenge ahead: “I dreamed too big.” Then she smiled. Because with the Route du Rhum approaching, the dream has become very real. Barrier, naturally, is already dreaming a little bigger. “In my dreams, if the magic happens, reaching the podium would be amazing,” she said. “It’s also important to allow yourself to dream big.” Nobody knows that better than Barrier.

item.title: Five shot dead at residence in Georgia's Douglas, police says
item.description: Five people were shot dead at a residence in Douglas, Georgia, on October 9, the city's police department said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Five people were shot dead at a residence in Douglas, Georgia, on October 9, the city's police department said on Saturday. Officers with the Douglas Police Department responded late on Friday to a report of shots fired and found five people with gunshot wounds who were all pronounced dead, according to a police statement. The investigation remains ongoing, the department added.

item.title: Russian attack on Ukrainian city kills 12, a day after Trump eases diesel sanctions on Moscow
item.description: Twelve people, including three children, were killed in a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Saturday, a day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel in a major setback for Kyiv.
item.dc:creator: Sergiy Chalyi, Max Hunder
item.content:encoded: Twelve people, including three children, were killed in a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Saturday, a day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel in a major setback for Kyiv. A six-year-old girl was among those killed when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled it from the wreckage. "Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, in some of his sharpest criticism yet of the White House. Fourteen others were wounded in the attack on Zaporizhzhia, an industrial city whose outskirts lie less than 30 km (20 miles) from the frontline. The bombardment was the latest in a series of recent high-casualty strikes across Ukraine. Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes over two days earlier this week. "Her birthday would have been at the end of the month," Anatoliy Chumniy, the grandfather of the six-year-old girl, said through tears. Local governor Mykhailo Semikin said Russia hit several locations simultaneously in the early hours of Saturday. Rescuers clambered through crumbled masonry to pull other residents of the building out alive. One man, whose leg was trapped in the rubble, screamed in pain as he was being freed. Zaporizhzhia, with a pre-war population of over 700,000, has been a regular target of Russian bombardment with strikes [USN:L8N43Z01W TEXT:"intensifying in the past few months"]. "Last night became yet another confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed," Zelenskiy said. TRUMP LIFTS DIESEL SANCTIONS Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports comes as his administration seeks to curb fuel prices, which have risen sharply during the US conflict with Iran. Kyiv had instead urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow in an effort to force it into serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war . Trump, meanwhile, has criticised Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he claims have driven up global prices. Kyiv has said it wants a total halt on all energy strikes by both sides as Moscow pummels Ukraine's power grid. On Saturday, parts of Kyiv and the surrounding region were left without power, bringing the city's metro trains to a complete halt for the second time this week. The latest strikes came after Ukrainian and European officials held talks with US negotiators in Miami on Friday aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to [USN:FWN45V1JO TEXT:"a person familiar with the discussions"]. Trump announced the diesel deal while the negotiations were underway, a move Zelenskiy said caught Kyiv by surprise. Russian President Vladimir Putin said after a call with Trump that an immediate resumption of peace talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow. Four civilians were killed and five others were wounded as a result of Ukrainian attacks on the [USN:S8N42201C TEXT:"Russian-controlled Luhansk region"] in eastern Ukraine, the Russian-installed governor said on Saturday. Reuters could not independently verify the report and there was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

item.title: NHL roundup: Capitals win as Rangers G Igor Shesterkin injured
item.description: Boone Jenner scored the tiebreaking goal late in the second period and the host Washington Capitals won 3-1 on Friday, cooling off the New York Rangers, who lost star goaltender Igor Shesterkin to a lower-body injury.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Boone Jenner scored the tiebreaking goal late in the second period and the host Washington Capitals won 3-1 on Friday, cooling off the New York Rangers, who lost star goaltender Igor Shesterkin to a lower-body injury. Timothy Liljegren also scored, Tom Wilson added an empty-netter and Logan Thompson made 22 saves for Washington, which has won three of its first four on the season. The Capitals also snapped the Rangers' four-game winning streak. Shesterkin, who entered with a 3-1-0 record, a 1.75 goals-against average and a .926 save percentage this season, appeared to awkwardly jam his right skate into the goalpost while sliding into position to make a save with 11:40 remaining in the second period of a 1-1 contest. The former Vezina Trophy winner, who stopped 13 of the 14 shots he saw on Friday, remained down on the ice for several minutes and had to be helped to the bench by a pair of teammates. Backup Dylan Garand, who made 22 saves in New York's 2-0 win at Detroit on Oct. 2, replaced Shesterkin and stopped 11 of 12 shots. Blue Jackets 3, Penguins 2 (SO) Kent Johnson scored in the first round of the shootout and Cam Talbot made it stand up in his season debut, fueling host Columbus to a victory over Pittsburgh. All four games between the teams last season ventured past regulation before Friday's game followed suit. Columbus defenseman Damon Severson collected a goal and an assist in his season debut. Mathieu Olivier also scored and Cole Sillinger notched two assists for the Blue Jackets. Pittsburgh's Bryan Rust scored for the second time in as many games and Evgeni Malkin also tallied. Sergei Murashov turned aside 43 shots for the Penguins, who have lost three in a row (0-2-1). Ducks 5, Jets 1 Judd Caulfield, Tim Washe and Mikael Granlund each had a goal and an assist for Anaheim in a victory at Winnipeg. Sam Colangelo and Nikita Nesterenko also scored, Jeff Malott and Beckett Sennecke contributed two assists apiece, and Lukas Dostal made 15 saves for the Ducks, who were coming off their first loss of the season. Kyle Connor scored and Clay Stevenson made 12 saves in his seventh NHL start for the Jets, who had won three in a row following a season-opening overtime defeat. Kraken 6, Red Wings 3 Frederick Gaudreau scored two of Seattle's four straight second-period goals as the Kraken pulled away against host Detroit. Ben Meyers supplied a goal and two assists, while Berkly Catton had a goal and an assist. Mackie Samoskevich and Vince Dunn also scored for the Kraken, while Philipp Grubauer made 37 saves. William Wallinder and Michael Brandsegg-Nygard scored their first NHL goals for Detroit. Viktor Arvidsson scored for the third straight game. --Field Level Media

item.title: French policing under scrutiny as student protest injuries mount
item.description: Fourteen-year-old Eden suffered a broken jaw and multiple smashed teeth when he was struck by a tear gas canister directed towards him at close range by a police officer last week during student protests in France, his parents and family lawyer said.
item.dc:creator: Juliette Jabkhiro, Layli Foroudi
item.content:encoded: Fourteen-year-old Eden suffered a broken jaw and multiple smashed teeth when he was struck by a tear gas canister directed towards him at close range by a police officer last week during student protests in France, his parents and family lawyer said. The teenager had been sitting on a wall looking at his phone metres away from the protest in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumone, the lawyer said. An officer approached him and struck him with a baton, prompting Eden to respond with a kick, according to the local prosecutor. A second officer then fired a tear gas grenade with a Cougar launcher, hitting him in the face. "(The officer) shot him in the mouth and left him lying on the ground, without even calling the emergency services," said lawyer Elsa Marcel. The family, who asked for Eden's second name to be withheld to protect their privacy, has filed a complaint for attempted murder, she said. A police spokesperson said they do not comment on ongoing investigations. The prosecutor's office said in a statement that the student had confronted the police and the officers tried to push him back. The officer was placed under formal investigation on charges of assault by a public official resulting in permanent disability or disfigurement on Tuesday, eight days after the incident. The case is one of 24 under investigation by the IGPN internal police watchdog linked to the policing of a more-than-two-week-long wave of [USN:L8N45S08G TEXT:"student unrest"] over [USN:L6N45M1EJ TEXT:"conditions"] in schools. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has described the demonstrations as the most violent in decades. The police response has renewed calls for the withdrawal of the use of rubber bullets and grenade launchers, which are not used by police in many other European countries and have been repeatedly criticised in recent years by rights groups, including Amnesty International and UN human rights experts, as dangerous and disproportionate. It has also sparked anger among the public and fanned support for a protest movement that is the latest manifestation of deep-seated [USN:L8N45L0FB TEXT:"discontent"] with President Emmanuel Macron’s government ahead of a 2027 election. Via interviews and reviews of legal documents, Reuters has documented 28 cases of injuries suffered due to police force, of which 15 are among those under investigation by the IGPN. They involve the use of rubber bullets, stun grenades, tear gas, batons and charges on horseback. In two cases, a person's eye has been lost or injured due to rubber bullets. In another, a 15-year-old in Lens had his hand blown off — likely by a stun grenade, according to interior minister Laurent Nunez, who [USN:L1N45T0B2 TEXT:"paused"] the use of stun grenades pending an investigation into the case. Nunez said on Wednesday in a radio interview that about 200 students had been injured, but that it was very rarely the result of police action. “Our primary role is, of course, to protect high school students,” he said. Authorities said that 700 police officers have also been injured, schools have been burned or ransacked, and teachers and members of the public have been attacked. The police have arrested 6,877 people, mostly minors. “France is an anomaly in terms of its use of arms and the number of victims — we have four irreversible injuries in the space of 12 days, and they are minors,” said Sebastian Roche, researcher on policing at the French National Centre for Scientific Research. “It is a level that is unknown in (France’s) contemporary history,” he said. CALLS TO BAN 'LESS LETHAL' WEAPONS Roche said that France stands out in Europe for its use of "less lethal" weapons such as rubber bullets and stun grenades. Such weapons are generally not used for public order policing in Britain, Italy and Germany, aside from Hamburg, and although permitted in Spain, have caused fewer injuries than in France, said Roche. In the Paris suburb of Argenteuil, a 16-year-old student on his way home after finding his school closed was shot by police, injuring his left eye, which may be permanently damaged, his lawyer Sophia Kerbaa told Reuters. It is not clear if he was hit by a rubber bullet or something else, she added. A video viewed by Reuters showed the boy bleeding from his eye. “He was in the wrong place at the wrong time ... he is injured and in shock,” Kerbaa said. The prosecutor investigating the case said that, according to the police account, the injured student “seemed to correspond” to one of two young people who had directed fireworks at police officers, who responded with rubber bullets. The interior ministry did not respond to questions on the case, or that of Eden. Human rights advocates, including Amnesty International, and some politicians have called for “less lethal” weapons to be banned permanently, while police unions say the police need these weapons to enforce order in violent situations and to ensure their own security. “We must withdraw the use of rubber bullets and ... aim for zero injured students. That will allow us to de-escalate,” Mayor Bally Bagayoko of the left-wing France Unbowed party [USN:L6N45T13Z TEXT:"told Reuters"]. Bagayoko joined the protests in his town Saint-Denis, saying he wanted to protect young people from the police. Thierry Clair, a police union representative, said that serious injuries such as Eden’s, or another child losing his hand, were tragedies, but should not call into question France’s policing techniques. He said the problem came instead from the intensity of the violence being committed by some young people who stoked tensions. “How do we respond when people are moving towards confrontation? If we remove intermediate force options, all we are left with is lethal force,” Clair told Reuters. “That is simply inconceivable.”

item.title: Germany's firewall against the far-right AfD feels the heat
item.description: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's warning this week that extremism was entering Germany's parliamentary system was the latest in a series of signs that mainstream parties' "firewall" to isolate the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has begun to buckle.
item.dc:creator: James Mackenzie, Andreas Rinke
item.content:encoded: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's [USN:L8N45T15N TEXT:"warning"] this week that extremism was entering Germany's parliamentary system was the latest in a series of signs that mainstream parties' "firewall" to isolate the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has begun to buckle. This week, at least four lawmakers from mainstream parties in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt appear to have defied party orders and voted to give the AfD, which wants to restrict immigration and restore energy ties with Russia, its first regional assembly speaker. The ballot was secret but suspicion immediately fell on the 15 members of Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) in parliament, who had been told to abstain. Karin Prien, deputy chair of the national CDU, said if CDU lawmakers were to blame, "there must be consequences". The AfD itself, which has been leading the CDU in nationwide surveys for more than a year and declared its aim of winning a national election due in 2029, hailed a "political turning point". "For the first time, it was clear that the so-called 'firewall' doesn't have to be stronger than the freedom of action of members of parliament," said Martin Reichardt, head of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt. COULD AFD WIN A NATIONAL ELECTION IN GERMANY? The AfD's [USN:L1N44Y01V TEXT:"record victory"] last month has alarmed rivals, who consider it an anti-democratic party opposed to the values that helped Germany to rebuild after World War Two and renounce the horrors of Nazism and its nationalist, racist ideology. The AfD rejects their label of "extreme right" as a slur. Across Europe and beyond, the result, which left the AfD just short of an absolute majority in the state parliament, was seen as one of the clearest indications yet that it could win a national election in 2029. Merz's coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats in Berlin has been under increasing strain, riven by disagreements and sliding in opinion polls as voters, like many across Western Europe, blame the mainstream parties for declining living standards. On Wednesday, the parties held talks to iron out differences over issues including pensions and tax, and said they were "determined not to hand our country over to extremists". Set up over a decade ago during the euro zone debt crisis, the AfD has grown from a fringe movement into the most popular party in Germany in opinion polls. Yet parts of the AfD - including its Saxony-Anhalt branch - have been designated as extremist by German security services, meaning that they are considered to be opposed to constitutional principles of human rights, democracy and the rule of law. The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), the domestic intelligence agency, compiled a 1,100-page confidential report last year that found the AfD incited resentment of migrants, as well as racism and Islamophobia. For its part, the AfD says it is restoring German national pride and values, and ensuring that migrants are not prioritised at the expense of German citizens. So far, the "firewall" approach - under which the established parties have refused to cooperate with the AfD - has kept it from joining any coalition government. In Saxony-Anhalt, where it needs three more seats for a majority, it is still [USN:L8N45S000 TEXT:"unclear"] how it can form a government after talks over a possible coalition with the populist far-left BSW made no progress. FEARS OF COOPERATION WITH AFD However, the AfD's Ulrich Siegmund, who dismisses the firewall as "childish", says he can persuade enough members of other parties to defy party orders to enable him to be confirmed as [USN:L8N4500A1 TEXT:"state premier"] by the end of the year. In this week's speaker ballot, the AfD's Tobias Rausch won 48 votes - four more than the combined total held by the AfD and the BSW. Merz has ruled out any arrangement with the AfD, which he says aims to destroy the CDU, and the issue is expected to be discussed at a CDU's leadership meeting on Sunday and Monday. But whether it remains realistic to refuse to cooperate with a party attracting almost a third of the vote, and more in the formerly communist eastern states where it is strongest, has become an urgent question. CDU deputy leader Prien said any sign of accommodation could open divisions that could "jeopardise the very existence of the entire party". The AfD has gained ground nationwide but remains weaker in western Germany than in the east, and appears unlikely to repeat its Saxony-Anhalt result in state elections next year. However, the problems that have helped create the conditions for its rapid rise resist easy answers. War in Ukraine has cut off the supply of cheap energy that fuelled Germany's economy while competition from China has eaten away at its once-invincible industrial base. Economists warn continually that fundamental reforms are needed to pensions and taxes to meet the needs of an ageing population, while deep divisions remain between the eastern and western regions, almost four decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall. Marking the anniversary last week of German reunification in 1990, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier acknowledged that many felt overlooked by the political system and that a generalised feeling of insecurity had undermined confidence. But, in an unusually bleak assessment, he said the bitter political climate was threatening to send Germany back into the chaos that ended the democracy of the prewar Weimar Republic. "Today is about the survival of democracy," he said. "We must stand up for what remains important."

item.title: New Zealand's O'Rourke ruled out of India series
item.description: New Zealand fast-bowler Will O'Rourke will miss the series against India as he continues his rehabilitation from injuries to his left hamstring and calf, the country's cricket board said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: New Zealand fast-bowler Will O'Rourke will miss the series against India as he continues his rehabilitation from injuries to his left hamstring and calf, the country's cricket board said on Saturday. O'Rourke suffered a hamstring tear during New Zealand's test series win over England in June, before hurting his calf in training in late August. The 25-year-old will aim to return to full fitness ahead of a four-test tour of neighbours Australia beginning on December 9. "It's obviously disappointing for Will to have to miss such a marquee tour at home against India," New Zealand coach Rob Walter said in a statement. "He was set to feature in both the ODI and test series, but following subsequent discussions, we all agreed it was best for him to take some more time to rehabilitate both injuries and safely build up his bowling loads. "Our pace bowling resources will be critical over the next few months so we're taking a conservative approach to Will's return to ensure he's fully fit before he takes the field again." New Zealand host India in five Twenty20 internationals, five one-day internationals and two tests, with the opening T20 in Christchurch on October 22.

item.title: Kyle Busch's 11-year-old son does burnouts at Charlotte memorial event
item.description: Brexton Busch honored his late father, Kyle Busch, in an appropriate manner during a celebration of life on Friday, doing burnouts at Charlotte Motor Speedway.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Brexton Busch honored his late father, Kyle Busch, in an appropriate manner during a celebration of life on Friday, doing burnouts at Charlotte Motor Speedway. The youngster was behind the wheel of the No. 8 Richard Childress Racing Chevrolet when he drove in front of 10,000-plus fans and performed burnouts until the rear tires went flat. Brexton Busch then climbed onto the roof of the car and acknowledged the crowd. His 4-year-old sister, Lennix, handed him a checkered flag, which Brexton then waved atop the car while taking a bow -- his father's signature victory celebration. Kyle Busch died unexpectedly on May 21 at age 41 of complications from severe bacterial pneumonia and sepsis. During the Friday event, Kyle Busch's brother Kurt, also a NASCAR champion, team owner Joe Gibbs and drivers including Austin Dillon and Kyle Larson discussed Kyle Busch's legacy. Samantha Busch, Kyle's widow, was the last to speak. "I keep thinking how lucky I was to know every single version of him, the young racer who took me around Indianapolis Motor Speedway when I was just 21 years old, and little did we know, it'd be the ride of our lifetime," Samantha Busch said. "The fierce competitor who basically thought second was last, and threw our kids ridiculously high in the air, a tradition that they loved and I feared every single time. The team owner who gave others a chance, Rowdy who loved his fans more than anything, and of course, stirring up things, and the dad who found so much joy and pride in his children. ... "This is not the end of Kyle's story. His story continues every time we give a young racer a chance, share something he taught us, or tell the next generation what made Rowdy unforgettable. Years from now, I hope people remember Kyle as one of NASCAR's greatest drivers. He worked his entire life for that. But I also hope they meet someone whose life is better because Kyle was here." Kyle Busch won the NASCAR Cup Series championship in 2015 and 2019. His total of 234 victories in NASCAR's top three series, including 63 in the Cup Series, is an all-time record. RCR has paused use of the No. 8 Chevrolet after Kyle Busch's death, saying the number is reserved for use by Brexton Busch "when he is ready to go NASCAR racing." --Field Level Media

item.title: Indian police detain 'cockroach' movement founder Abhijeet Dipke
item.description: CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were also detained.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Police in the Indian capital Delhi detained the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, Abhijeet Dipke, on Saturday, ahead of a protest called by the youth movement demanding the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner, the party said. TV channels reported earlier that police officers met Dipke at the Delhi airport after he arrived from the financial capital Mumbai and asked him to call off the protest as authorities had banned it. CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were also detained from their flight upon landing, the movement said in a statement.

item.title: Jocelyn Bioh on why Broadway is finally ready for 'School Girls'
item.description: The playwright and actor talks beauty, colorism, and how Broadway has changed in the decade since she wrote the play.
item.dc:creator: Kathryn Lurie
item.content:encoded:
Playwright Jocelyn Bioh during an interview with Reuters in New York City. REUTERS/Brendan McDermid Nearly a decade after Jocelyn Bioh wrote “School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play,” the play itself has barely changed. But the world around it has. The comedy about a group of teenage girls at a Ghanaian boarding school premiered off-Broadway in 2017, launching Bioh’s career as a playwright and going on to become a hit at regional theaters across the United States. But despite its success, Bioh was told it might not belong on Broadway. Now “School Girls” has made it there — following the Broadway success of Bioh’s “Jaja’s African Hair Braiding” in 2023 — and she is finding an audience that responds differently to the play’s exploration of body image, the privileging of lighter skin, known as colorism, and the often brutal social dynamics of girlhood. Beneath its rapid-fire jokes and teenage rivalries is a more painful story about who gets to be considered beautiful — and what people are willing to do to fit that ideal. Speaking in New York City, Bioh discusses what has changed since “School Girls” was first produced, the universality of teenage insecurity and why bringing the play to Broadway feels like coming full circle. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

How does it feel to finally bring “School Girls” to Broadway? It feels incredibly humbling. This play changed my life. It was the first play of mine that ever got produced. I can very clearly mark what my life was like before opening night of that show and then after. That audiences and critics all still feel the same way nearly a decade later is a reminder that I was on the right track. It also feels doubly exciting because even though it had so much success regionally and has been all over the country, I was told, “It's a great play, but maybe it's not the right fit for a Broadway stage.”

What do you think was meant by that, and what has changed enough for it to be on Broadway now? Broadway shows were very specific then. They didn't have ensembles that looked like the cast of “School Girls.” It was a lot of celebrities, a lot of things that seemed to fit into one specific category or box. The world has shifted. Audiences are different than they were 10 years ago. In a lot of ways, “Jaja's African Hair Braiding” having so much success was a marker that, a Broadway play is just a play that's on Broadway. It doesn't necessarily have to fit a specific category.

Is there anything in the play that hits differently than it did when you first wrote it? The conversation around beauty standards and body image has shifted in the last 10 years. Some would say (for the) better, some would say worse, but we're all aware of it in a different way. The play kicks off with Paulina bullying Nana about her size and her eating. You can feel the audience is immediately on Nana's side. Halfway through the play, she has a moment where she really stands up to Paulina, and every night that moment gets applause. You can feel the audience cheering, almost jumping up ready to fight with her. They're taking off their earrings! We did not have that experience off-Broadway. I think we were in a time where we accepted the idea that if you were somebody who was bigger, you should be losing weight; you should be trying to conform. Our ideas of beauty are very different now. Big ships turn slow, but I appreciate that I can feel that in the audience. Did you rewrite much for this production? Very small things, little jokes that I thought would land better. But the play is still largely the same thing I wrote in 2016. If I were sitting down to write this play now, I don't know that I would be as honest or as vulnerable as I was then, particularly in the moments where Paulina is speaking very directly about how colorism has affected her life. I think I would censor myself a little bit now. I never thought the play would get produced, so I was very free and vulnerable in a way.

Playwright Jocelyn Bioh. REUTERS/Brendan McDermid Why? When you're a playwright and your name starts to grow within the community, you start to have an awareness of the responsibility of your words. And I'm okay with having that responsibility because I know I'm doing something really different. I'm really blowing open how people see Black and African people on a theatrical stage. There's an incredible responsibility to that. The play takes place in Ghana, but these girls feel instantly recognizable. Did you know when you were writing it how universal they would be? I understood that there's a real rich universality we have, particularly in school and friendship dynamics. Those things are evergreen and universal. I knew what I was writing was different, (that) the girls and the people I was reflecting were different, but I didn't want to alienate audiences. That's part of why I added the subtitle. What's something we all know and recognize about the teenage experience? Mean girls. Paulina seems to believe that if she can just become Miss Ghana, she can escape the limits of her life. Is her obsession with beauty really an obsession with power and possibility? Probably. Ultimately, I think she really believes this is going to set her up for a successful life in entertainment. The play is set in 1986, and if you became Miss Ghana, Miss World, Miss Universe — any of those things — you could become a star. This is how we have Vanessa Williams or Halle Berry or Kenya Moore, if you're of the “Real Housewives” persuasion. (Another character,) Eloise, is a former Miss Ghana and did leave. She's come back now living a different life, (signifying that) in order to have success, you've got to get out. In order to have power, you have to get out. Maybe Paulina doesn't see the beauty and power that she can build in her own country. That's reflective of so many immigrant, particularly African immigrant, stories: In order to have success, you need to leave. I don't know if the play were set in 2026, (if) that would be the case now. I think the play would be very different. But for Paulina and her circumstances then, that is what she believed. The play deals so directly with colorism. Do you think colorism is in some ways more sensitive to talk about than racism? They're inextricably linked. The play largely talks about and shows the effects of colorism, but then ends with a global lesson on racism. And we've not moved on from it. When we started rehearsals for the play in August, the biggest news story was Lupita Nyong'o playing Helen of Troy in Christopher Nolan's film (“The Odyssey”). (Her casting) did not fit with whomever's standard of beauty (for) the woman whose face launched a thousand ships. Why didn't it fit? Why were there so many suggestions about, “Well, Zendaya's in the movie, why can't she play that part?” That's a very clear conversation about colorism, whether people are using that word or not.

When I wrote this play, it was really important for me to have that conversation because it had affected my life so much. Revisiting it now, especially in relation to these conversations that are happening globally, I'm like, well, we've not moved on from it. We can't move on from colorism because nobody's moved on from racism. I can't change people's minds. But if people come to see “School Girls” and their implicit bias can shift just a little bit, then I've done my job. The play is extremely funny until you realize how much pain is sitting underneath the humor. How deliberate is that? I really believe that comedy is just a funny way of being serious. Humor and pain are on two different sides of a truth coin. It's all rooted in truth. Paulina is a girl in the world who's trying to be affirmed and validated that she belongs there, that her beauty is widely accepted even if she knows that it's not. The lengths she goes to get there are what's comical, but it's rooted in something real that we all experience. At the end of the day, I'm a comedic writer and I want people to be entertained. But because I know the responsibility of who I'm introducing and the culture I'm introducing, I think there's a responsibility in also educating people. If I can make that medicine go down with a little bit of sugar, honey, agave, whatever you like, I'm willing to go there. The perspectives expressed in Culture Current are the subject’s own and do not necessarily reflect the views of Reuters News.

item.title: Trackhouse's Fernandez takes first pole at Indonesian GP
item.description: Trackhouse rider Raul Fernandez grabbed a career-first pole at the Indonesian Grand Prix on Saturday, with title contenders Jorge Martin and Marc Marquez set to start on the second row.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Trackhouse rider Raul Fernandez grabbed a career-first pole at the Indonesian Grand Prix on Saturday, with title contenders Jorge Martin and Marc Marquez set to start on the second row. Fernandez, who won the British MotoGP in August, finished quickest with a lap of one minute 28.852 seconds -- 0.109 quicker than Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi. "Too many times, I was very close to taking pole (in the past)," said Fernandez, who also set a lap record during practice on Friday. "Yesterday, I started to feel super comfortable with the bike. This morning, to be honest, I didn't really feel like that. "I just tried to be calm, tried to not be nervous. Now we have a very good opportunity, let's try to enjoy and let's try to fight for the victory." VR46 Racing's Fabio Di Giannantonio completed the front row with a strong display on his birthday. Bezzecchi was content with second place despite having to abandon what looked set to be a pole-winning lap when yellow flags were waved following a Fermin Aldeguer crash. "I'm very happy. It was a good job this morning in practice, but also in the qualifying, I was confident on the bike," the Italian said. "Unfortunately, I met a yellow flag in the second stint, but I'm very, very happy, satisfied. It's a very good first row for this afternoon, but also for tomorrow." Defending champion Marquez of Ducati was fourth-quickest, just ahead of title rival and championship leader Martin of Aprilia. With six rounds remaining in the season, including the Indonesian MotoGP, the outcome of the championship is hanging on a knife-edge as Martin sits on 333 points - just two above Marquez. Marquez will fancy his chances of closing that gap this weekend, but the weight of history is against him, with the Spaniard having a disastrous record at the Mandalika circuit, where he has never completed a full MotoGP race. Last year, he suffered a season-ending collarbone injury in the race after a crunching collision with Bezzecchi on the opening lap.

item.title: Washington QB Demond Williams Jr. exits Iowa game due to injury
item.description: Washington quarterback Demond Williams Jr. missed the start of the second half against No. 20 Iowa on Friday due to an apparent left shoulder injury.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Washington quarterback Demond Williams Jr. missed the start of the second half against No. 20 Iowa on Friday due to an apparent left shoulder injury. Williams got hurt while being tackled late in the first half and was undergoing X-rays as the third quarter began, coach Jedd Fisch told sideline reporters. Elijah Brown, who replaced Williams late in the second quarter, led the Huskies to a touchdown on the opening drive of the second half, cutting the Hawkeyes' lead to 27-10. Williams completed 6 of 11 passes for 69 yards before exiting. The junior owns a 66.7% completion rate and 1,396 passing yards with eight touchdowns and three interceptions through six games this season. In his three seasons at Washington, Williams has a 70.1% completion rate, 5,405 passing yards, 41 TD passes and 12 interceptions in 32 games. --Field Level Media

item.title: Defenseman Mathew Dumba, 13-year NHL vet, retires at age 32
item.description: Veteran defenseman Mathew Dumba announced his retirement on Friday after 13 NHL seasons.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Veteran defenseman Mathew Dumba announced his retirement on Friday after 13 NHL seasons. A first-round selection (seventh overall) of Minnesota in the 2012 NHL Draft, Dumba played 10 seasons for the Wild. The winner of the 2019-20 King Clancy Memorial Trophy, which is given annually for leadership qualities on and off the ice and humanitarian work in the community, played 11 games for the Pittsburgh Penguins in 2025-26 before his contract was terminated in April. "Matt Dumba is officially hanging up his skates after 748 NHL career games," the NHL Players Association posted on social media Friday. "Wishing the former blue liner and 2019-20 King Clancy Memorial Trophy winner the best of luck in his retirement!" The 32-year-old Regina, Saskatchewan, native tallied 261 points (85 goals, 176 assists) with the Wild (2013-14 to 2022-23), Arizona Coyotes (2023-24), Tampa Bay Lightning (2023-24), Dallas Stars (2024-25) and Pittsburgh. He produced five goals and 10 assists in 54 career playoff games, 49 of which came with Minnesota. He notched career highs in goals (14), assists (36) and points (50) during the 2017-18 season. --Field Level Media

item.title: India unveils tough curbs on dollar demand to defend rupee
item.description: India on Saturday unveiled fresh measures to shore up the rupee, redirecting oil companies' dollar purchases away from the spot market and tightening hedging rules as the currency hovers near record lows.
item.dc:creator: Jaspreet Kalra, Nimesh Vora
item.content:encoded: India on Saturday unveiled fresh measures to shore up the rupee, redirecting oil companies' dollar purchases away from the spot market and tightening hedging rules as the currency hovers near record lows. The steps by the Reserve Bank of India come as persistent pressure on the rupee, fuelled by surging oil prices and global bond yields, has driven the currency down more than 7% this year. The central bank will open a special window to meet the daily dollar requirements of three state-run oil-marketing companies, easing pressure on the spot market. Under such an arrangement, used during periods of currency stress, the RBI provides oil companies dollars directly from its foreign exchange reserves. Indian Oil (IOC.NS) , Hindustan Petroleum (HPCL.NS) and Bharat Petroleum (BPCL.NS) will be allowed to access the facility from Monday, the RBI said. "Addressing oil companies' dollar requirements removes one of the largest sources of demand from the FX market, which should help reduce volatility but it will show up in a depletion of reserves," said Dhiraj Nim, FX strategist at ANZ Bank in Mumbai. After the steps were announced, the rupee strengthened by about 0.6% against the dollar in the non-deliverable forward market, albeit in thin trading. CURBING HEDGING PRESSURE Elevated demand for protection against further rupee losses has weighed on the currency in recent months, with [USN:L1N45R06L TEXT:"importers' appetite"] for dollars far exceeding exporter supply. The central bank has responded by tightening rules on speculative corporate activity and raising the cost of protection against further rupee weakness. The RBI is "trying to moderate potentially destabilising derivative demand, improve the integrity of underlying exposure verification and discourage circumvention through multiple transactions or repeated rebooking," a person familiar with the central bank's thinking said, commenting on condition of anonymity as they are not authorized to speak to the media. The central bank has mandated that forex dealers maintain a 20% "foreign exchange risk reserve" on derivative contracts used to buy foreign currency against the rupee, for the purposes of hedging current account transactions. The requirement applies to transactions with a notional value exceeding $2 million. The reserve requirement will lift the cost of buying protection against further rupee weakness, helping to discourage excessive hedging, two bankers said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Chinese authorities have previously used similar tools to discourage one-way bets against the yuan. India's central bank has also slashed the limits on the size of derivative transactions users can undertake without proof of underlying exposure to $5 million from $100 million. The lower cap applies across all derivative products, including exchange-traded futures. The measures follow more than $140 billion in capital inflows raised through one-off policy steps to encourage overseas FX deposits alongside offshore borrowing by state-run firms and banks. Yet despite those inflows, sustained central bank intervention and a [USN:L1N45T036 TEXT:"rate hike"] earlier this week, the rupee remains under pressure. The steps should temper, but not eliminate, pressure on the rupee, ANZ's Nim said. "The underlying drivers, including oil prices and capital flows, remain, and the real test will be how reserves and the rupee behave in the coming week," Nim added.

item.title: Taiwan won't give up freedom, Lai says; Beijing slams 'ulterior motives'
item.description: Taiwan cherishes peace but will not give up its freedom, and there must be respect for the right of Taiwan's people to exist, President Lai Ching-te said on Saturday in a National Day speech, adding that boosting defences is not a provocation.
item.dc:creator: Yimou Lee, Ben Blanchard
item.content:encoded: Taiwan cherishes peace but will not give up its freedom, and there must be respect for the right of Taiwan's people to exist, President Lai Ching-te said on Saturday in a National Day speech, adding that boosting defences is not a provocation. Beijing quickly denounced the speech, saying it "distorts the truth" and reveals "ulterior motives." Democratically governed Taiwan has faced increased military and political pressure from China, which views the island as its own territory over the strong objections of the government in Taipei. Facing China's far larger military, which is adding advanced new weapons such as stealth-fighter jets, aircraft carriers and a huge array of missiles, Taiwan is ramping up [USN:L4N44V0I5 TEXT:"defence spending"] and modernising its armed forces. Peace cannot rely solely on "wishes", Lai said outside the Presidential Office. "Taiwan cherishes peace, but we will not give up our freedom. We are open to exchanges, but will not accept subordination." Taiwan's resolve is not only a matter of its survival in the face of "authoritarian expansion", he added. "It is about whether the international community still believes that force cannot override rules, and that the powerful cannot strip a people of their right to determine their own future." DEFENCE INVESTMENT NOT 'PROVOCATION' China's Taiwan Affairs Office said Lai's speech "disregards facts, distorts the truth, misleads the public, and reveals ulterior motives", accusing him of stubbornly clinging to "Taiwan independence" separatist thinking and exaggerating the "threat from the mainland". "There is only one China in the world, and Taiwan is part of China – this is the true status quo in the Taiwan Strait," the office said. Taiwan's future "can and must be decided jointly by all the Chinese people, including our compatriots in Taiwan," China's state television CCTV reported the office's spokesperson as saying. China, which has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, calls the president a "separatist" and has rebuffed his offers of talks. The US welcomes Lai's commitment to maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, a senior US administration official said, adding, in reference to China, that "a routine speech is no justification for aggressive or coercive actions". The United States is Taiwan's most important international backer despite the lack of formal diplomatic ties. Lai did not use his usual wording that neither side of the Taiwan Strait is "subordinate" to the other, but did use a phrase from Jesus' Sermon on the Mount, saying Taiwan must become a "'city upon a hill,' built with courage and confidence". Lai said his government's increased investment in defence aimed to deter war, not provoke it. "And we are strengthening our self-defence not to abandon dialogue, but to ensure that dialogue can take place on the basis of parity and dignity," he told the crowd at the event, where he also watched military displays and dancing performances. "There must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist." US YET TO APPROVE NEW ARMS PACKAGE In 2024, shortly after Lai's first National Day speech as president, China held war games around the island but did not do so last year. Its last [USN:L1N3Y000J TEXT:"war games"] near Taiwan were in late December, following news of an $11-billion US arms deal for Taipei, the largest ever. US President Donald Trump has yet to approve a second package, worth [USN:L1N45T00J TEXT:"$14 billion."] Lai said he welcomed the United States and China managing their competition through [USN:L6N45K195 TEXT:"dialogue"] and reducing the risk of conflict and war, in what a Taiwanese official told reporters was a direct response to last month's [USN:L1N45H0FW TEXT:"China-US summit"] in Washington. But Lai urged democracies in the Indo-Pacific region to join forces to retain the status quo of peace and stability in the region. Taiwan's National Day is held on the anniversary of a 1911 uprising that led to the overthrow of China's last imperial dynasty and the establishment of the Republic of China. The Republican government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing a civil war with Mao Zedong's communists, and the Republic of China remains the island's formal name.

item.title: Ducks bounce back, snap Jets' winning streak
item.description: Judd Caulfield, Tim Washe and Mikael Granlund each had a goal and an assist for the visiting Anaheim Ducks in a 5-1 win against the Winnipeg Jets on Friday night.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Judd Caulfield, Tim Washe and Mikael Granlund each had a goal and an assist for the visiting Anaheim Ducks in a 5-1 win against the Winnipeg Jets on Friday night. Sam Colangelo and Nikita Nesterenko also scored, Jeff Malott and Beckett Sennecke contributed two assists apiece, and Lukas Dostal made 15 saves for the Ducks, who were coming off a 5-2 loss to the visiting Edmonton Oilers on Wednesday after winning their first two games of the season. Kyle Connor scored, and Clay Stevenson made 12 saves in his seventh NHL start for the Jets, who had won three in a row following a season-opening overtime loss to the Boston Bruins. The Ducks kept their streak alive of scoring first in every game this season when Caulfield gave them a 1-0 lead at 14:41 of the first period. Malott drove to the net and Stevenson saved his backhand from in close, but Caulfield slid the rebound between his pads for his first NHL goal in his fourth game. The fourth line struck again in the second period when Washe finished off a feed from Malott on a 2-on-1 to make it 2-0 at 5:20. The assist gave Malott his first multipoint game in the NHL. Anaheim stretched the lead to 3-0 at 4:25 of the third. Sennecke drove toward the left post and then backhanded a short feed to Colangelo in front of the crease and he tapped the puck in the net. Sennecke has three goals and three assists through the first four games of his second season in the NHL.
