item.title: US lifts sanctions on daughter of Myanmar military-linked businessman
item.description: The United States lifted on Friday sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, according to the US Treasury Department's website, after she filed a suit seeking removal from the blacklist.
item.dc:creator: Simon Lewis
item.content:encoded: The United States lifted on Friday sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, according to the US Treasury Department's website, after she filed a suit seeking removal from the blacklist. The move comes after Reuters reported this week that the Trump administration had [USN:L6N45T16N TEXT:"opened talks with Myanmar's military-installed government"], reversing US policy that sought to isolate the generals who overthrew elected leaders in 2021. It was unclear if the decision to remove Myanmar national Theint Win Htet from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List) was a result of the talks. After the 2021 coup, former President Joe Biden's administration imposed sanctions on senior Myanmar military officers and companies it accused of providing support for the military junta, which triggered a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million. The Treasury in January 2024 [USN:S0N3D107F TEXT:"targeted the "][USN:S0N3D107F TEXT:"Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies"], its founder Thein Win Zaw and his family, saying the company imported and distributed petroleum on behalf of the military and that the family owned at least 20 companies closely associated with the regime. Thein Win Zaw's adult daughter, Theint Win Htet, sued the Biden administration seeking her removal from the SDN List, but her case was dismissed in February 2025. The sanctions freeze any US assets of those targeted and generally bar Americans from dealing with them. The US in July 2025 [USN:L1N3TM01T TEXT:"lifted sanctions"] on several other Myanmar nationals and a firm under sanctions for aiding the military. Theint Win Htet filed a new complaint in July this year, arguing that she has no active role in her father's business affairs, adding that the sanctions had interrupted her studies in the US, where she completed a bachelor's degree at New York University and was enrolled in a master's program at Columbia University. "Plaintiff’s US credit cards have been blocked, her foreign bank accounts have been restricted, closed, or refused, and she has been unable to complete her university studies in the United States," said the complaint by Theint Win Htet, who said in the complaint she now lives with her mother in Bangkok. Her mother was removed from the sanctions list last year. Campaign group Justice For Myanmar denounced the US move at a time when it said the Myanmar military was escalating attacks on civilians. "It is deplorable that the US government continues to delist Myanmar cronies and their family members that provide funding for the junta's terror," the group said. Theint Win Htet's lawyer, Washington-based sanctions specialist Erich Ferrari, filed a notice with the US District Court for the District of Columbia on Friday voluntarily dismissing the lawsuit after her delisting. Ferrari declined to comment.

item.title: India's TCS senior staff will miss out on variable pay for September quarter, memo shows
item.description: Senior staff at India's Tata Consultancy Services will miss out on quarterly bonuses after the company failed to meet performance targets, according to an internal memo seen by Reuters, the first time in at least two years all variable pay was withheld for some workers.
item.dc:creator: Sai B
item.content:encoded: Senior staff at India's Tata Consultancy Services (TCS.NS) will miss out on quarterly bonuses after the company failed to meet performance targets, according to an internal memo seen by Reuters, the first time in at least two years all variable pay was withheld for some workers. "For associates C3A grade and above, there will be no QVA (quarterly variable allowance) this quarter. This decision was taken after careful consideration as our performance for the quarter fell short of internal targets," said Sudeep Kunnumal, chief human resource officer in the memo. Associates in C3A and above grades are employees with typically 7-10 years of experience up to senior-level management. The junior-level employees will get 100% of the eligible pay, the memo added. Mails sent to TCS did not elicit a response. Employees, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said typically the company awards 50-100% of variable pay and it is the first time in at least two years that the company has explicitly said no bonuses shall be awarded. This comes as the country's largest IT firm reported its [USN:L6N45T0UF TEXT:"weakest"] September-quarter sequential revenue growth in three years, signaling continued pressure on traditional IT services demand even as AI-related revenue jumped nearly 20%. The uptick in AI revenue, however, was cheered by investors on Friday as the stock rose as much as 6.2%. India's $315 billion IT sector is also facing uncertainty stemming from the Trump administration as it [USN:S0N43501J TEXT:"suspended"] major IT outsourcers including TCS, Infosys (INFY.NS) , HCLTech (HCLT.NS) from a key green-card program on Thursday, widening a crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs.

item.title: Erik Prince's forces suffer battlefield loss in Congo, former UFC fighter among wounded, sources say
item.description: Popular former UFC fighter Tim Kennedy was among the wounded in an ambush that killed or wounded at least 20 people deployed by Vectus Global.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Donati
item.content:encoded: Blackwater founder Erik Prince's forces suffered a major battlefield loss in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-September when enemy forces ambushed them, killing and wounding at least 20 people, including a popular former UFC fighter, sources close to the government and his company said. The frontline clash shows how Prince, an ally and supporter of US President Donald Trump, has taken on an expanded role in Congo through his company Vectus Global. The company, which also operates in Haiti and other parts of Africa, provides consulting and security services and previously [USN:L6N3XA0X0 TEXT:"helped Congo’s army"] secure the city of Uvira in South Kivu against Rwanda-backed rebels who control swathes of the east. A veteran special operator reported on his podcast earlier this week that former US Green Beret and Ultimate Fighting Championship contestant Tim Kennedy was injured in Congo. The involvement of Prince's forces and the number of casualties have not previously been reported. The attack in South Kivu on September 17 left about 20 dead and wounded, two sources working with Congo's government said. The dead included at least seven Congolese and a former member of New Zealand's Special Forces, while the wounded included Kennedy and another foreign contractor, the sources said. A Vectus Global representative declined to comment. The company has not previously suffered casualties in Congo, a source with direct knowledge of the operation said. One of the sources who works for Congo's government said that Rwandan forces backing the M23 rebels may have surprised them by tracking a drone used for surveillance operations to their location. Spokespeople for the Congolese and Rwandan governments and for the M23 did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Kennedy, the former mixed martial arts fighter, survived the attack with three gunshot wounds to the leg, three sources said, and is being treated at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in the suburbs of Washington. Kennedy has a popular podcast channel and millions of followers on social media. Trump is a fan of UFC, [USN:L6N42N00Z TEXT:"hosting fights"] at the White House this year. The US State Department and Walter Reed declined to comment. Kennedy's parents did not respond to requests for comment. A Congolese security source, who said some 20 people were wounded and killed in the attack, added that villagers were likely among the casualties as well. Reuters spoke to at least 10 sources either with direct knowledge of the attack or briefed on the outcome. PRINCE TOOK EXPANDED ROLE IN CONGO'S CONFLICT Prince's initial mandate in Congo was to secure and improve revenue collection from the country's vast mineral reserves, which have been plundered for decades, fuelling relentless conflict in the east. But in January and early February, his forces deployed to Uvira after Washington helped broker a deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from the strategic town. The size of Prince's forces in Congo is unclear. One of the sources with direct knowledge of the attack said the Vectus team was travelling between locations when the ambush took place and its sophistication suggested Rwandan forces were involved. "It reinforces the need for DRC sovereignty to be restored. It's an incredibly dangerous place right now," the source said. Two other sources said the ambush was carried out by the Rwandan military. Prince is the founder of now-defunct private military firm Blackwater, some of whose members were pardoned in 2020 for killing Iraqi civilians. The State Department has said it does not have any contracts with Prince in Congo, though US officials have said they plan to work [USN:L1N43O0RW TEXT:"more closely with Vectus Global"] in Haiti. The deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from Uvira was part of [USN:L6N3XA0X0 TEXT:"wider agreements"] brokered by the Trump administration to try to end the conflict in eastern Congo. POPULAR PODCASTER Kennedy, a father of four, has posted his views on politics, culture, fitness and more on social media. He also runs a popular YouTube podcast in which he interviews UFC fighters, veterans, cultural disruptors and others. He has often posted about his family, including four young children. In late August, he posted about having "incredible conversations about what being a man means and what sacrifice really looks like" with his son. He did not disclose details about his upcoming trip to Congo. The United Nations and Western powers say Rwanda backs M23, even exercising command and control over the group. Rwanda denies this. Fighting in the decades-long conflict flared early last year, with M23 fighters making rapid gains in the east, which is rich in tantalum, gold, lithium and other minerals.

item.title: Anthropic discloses fake tip to police among new rogue AI incidents
item.description: An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false homicide tip to a Philadelphia police website, among a string of incidents the AI company disclosed on Friday detailing Claude models' unsanctioned manipulation of some government websites.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false homicide tip to a Philadelphia police website, among a string of incidents the AI company disclosed on Friday detailing Claude models' unsanctioned manipulation of some government websites. It is the first known instance in which a rogue AI appears to have tried to communicate a bogus tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive, while not explicitly barred from submitting forms. The cases are the latest examples of rogue or undesired behavior by the AI models of tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI. They add fuel to national concerns about the fast-advancing technology amid reports of corporate network hacks by AI agents, and researchers' warnings of an eventual existential threat to humanity. Many of the cases Anthropic revealed involved websites run by federal, state and local agencies. Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved, but did not disclose who those parties were. "Super intelligence companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm," FTC Director of Public Affairs Joe Gabriel Simonson said on X. This process was "not optional," he said, adding that the Super Intelligence Force would fulfill its responsibility. The FTC said Anthropic disclosed to the SI Force on Friday its late September discovery of incidents involving what the task force called "unauthorized and fraudulent use of government and other systems". TIP ATTRIBUTED TO AUTOMATED TEST PROCESS On Friday, Philadelphia police said Anthropic notified them of the spurious tip this week, and attributed the submissions to an automated testing process. "The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable," they said. The July 18 tip purported to come from someone who might have information about the case, police added. "I may have information regarding this case," Anthropic's model wrote in its submission. "I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around (the street named on the page) during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." The brackets featured in Anthropic's statement. Previous incidents have involved AI agents hacking into vulnerable systems or commandeering unsanctioned platforms to communicate with one another. In September, Anthropic rival OpenAI apologized for the hacking of an Australian health data portal by a rogue AI agent, the first known instance of an AI agent exploiting a government website. A BOGUS TIP In two cases described on Friday, Anthropic’s models obtained for free public data normally only available for a fee. Another instanced revealed an obscure flaw that allowed use of a public tool hosted by a university. Claude models were also able to bypass restrictions by using free services that shorten URLs. Philadelphia police said the tip "was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination." Knowingly giving false reports to law enforcement authorities is a misdemeanor under Pennsylvania law, which specifies "a person", however. This includes "information relating to an offense or incident when he knows he has no information relating to such offense or incident." Police quoted Anthropic as telling them the test process was stopped after discovery of the incident. The false tip was submitted through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com concerning an unsolved homicide. Police said they had no evidence of unauthorized access to their systems or compromise of their data.

item.title: Republican opposition widens to livestreamed execution; Trump still weighing it
item.description: Vice President JD Vance expressed skepticism over whether the Pentagon will proceed with livestreaming the execution.
item.dc:creator: Phil Stewart, Nandita Bose
item.content:encoded: Republican US lawmakers joined religious leaders and international observers on Friday in opposing a Pentagon plan to livestream an execution by firing squad, while President Donald Trump said he has not yet decided whether to allow the live feed. Vice President JD Vance expressed skepticism over whether the Pentagon will proceed with livestreaming the scheduled December 3 execution of former US Army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan, who was found guilty in a US military trial of fatally shooting 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. "I don't know that that's actually going to happen," Vance told reporters in Cincinnati, referring to the livestream plan championed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. If it is shown publicly, Vance said, "I'm not going to be watching it." Trump told reporters that Hasan deserves the death penalty by firing squad, calling him "totally nuts." But when asked if he wants the execution livestreamed, the Republican president said he has yet to "make a determination about that." A senior US Catholic bishop and a US evangelical Christian leader voiced opposition to the plan, as did the UN human rights office. REPUBLICANS VOICE CONCERN Several Republican US lawmakers argued against livestreaming. Senator John Curtis wrote on social media that "a civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment." Senator Thom Tillis and Representative Austin Scott said livestreaming executions is what Islamist extremists would do. Representative Rob Bresnahan said the pain felt by victims and family members "deserves respect, not a public show." "This should be reconsidered," Representative Michael Baumgartner wrote on social media. Democrats were overwhelmingly opposed. The event would be extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the US military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945. Hasan, now 56, is believed to be confined to a wheelchair, having been shot by police during his arrest. A senior White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Trump does not oppose the idea of livestreaming the execution but could change his mind. The White House is hearing concerns from lawmakers, allies and religious leaders who are urging the administration not to livestream it, the official said. Hegseth, a Trump appointee, confirmed the plans for the livestreamed execution on Thursday. 'A CULTURE OF DEATH' Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, condemned the planned livestream as a "barbaric promotion of a culture of death." Walter Kim, president of the National Association of Evangelicals, said on social media that a livestreamed execution by firing squad "risks turning one of the state's most solemn responsibilities into a public spectacle, promoting a culture of death, rather than a culture that upholds the dignity of every human being." Hegseth, a member of a conservative evangelical denomination, has made his Christian faith a hallmark of his tenure as defense secretary and has led prayer services at the Pentagon. He also has brushed off Pope Leo's criticism of the Iran war . Hasan, an American-born Muslim, said during his 2013 trial that he carried out the shootings to try to stop what he called a US war on Islam. "Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance told reporters. 'FREE PROPAGANDA' Joe Kent, who resigned this year as Trump's head of the National Counterterrorism Center, wrote on social media: "Streaming his execution is not just a stain on our morality — it also gives the terrorists free propaganda that they will use to radicalize & recruit more terrorists." Brendan Carr, chair of the Federal Communications Commission, told CNBC it is his understanding that the execution would not air on broadcast TV but said he would [USN:L1N45V0M1 TEXT:"defer"] to Hegseth on whether US networks could air it. US law [USN:L1N45V0IV TEXT:"prohibits the recording or broadcasting"] of executions in the federal prison system. Military regulations have not applied that same prohibition. Courts have rejected lawsuits brought by media organizations seeking broader public access to executions. The UN human rights office said public executions violate prohibitions against torture. "Public executions constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment," Shabia Mantoo, a spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, told a news briefing in Geneva. Amnesty International called the use of a firing squad "reprehensible." Mental health experts said it also could traumatize children. The execution is scheduled to be held at the same sprawling military base where Hasan opened fire with a handgun in a medical facility. The Pentagon on Friday declined to say whether families of those killed in Hasan's attack would be invited to attend the execution, as is common practice in US civilian executions. It remains unclear how the Army would select the shooters and what protocols might be followed during the execution itself. The Pentagon said it would release details later. The plan to livestream the execution comes at a time of heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following the [USN:L1N45M04O TEXT:"botched lethal injection"] last week of a Tennessee woman who was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder. The controversy has flared in the run-up to the November 3 US midterm elections in which Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.

item.title: Fuerte terremoto sacude Panamá, sin registros de destrucción masiva
item.description: Un terremoto de magnitud 7.7 sacudió el sur de Panamá el viernes, causando daños en edificios y dejando a miles de personas asustadas en las calles, pero el país aparentemente evitó una destrucción generalizada o víctimas mortales.
item.dc:creator: Elida Moreno, Dave Sherwood
item.content:encoded: Un terremoto de magnitud 7.7 sacudió el sur de Panamá el viernes, causando daños en edificios y dejando a miles de personas asustadas en las calles, pero el país aparentemente evitó una destrucción generalizada o víctimas mortales. El Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos (USGS, por su sigla en inglés) informó que el epicentro se ubicó en una zona poco poblada a unos 200 kilómetros (km) de la capital y a una profundidad de 12.6 km. En las horas siguientes, a pesar de que decenas de réplicas sacudieron el istmo, el Canal de Panamá informó que operaba con normalidad y el Aeropuerto Internacional de Tocumen levantó la suspensión de vuelos. Los oficinistas del exclusivo centro de negocios de Ciudad de Panamá -una urbe de unas 410,000 personas- se preocupaban por cómo regresar a casa en medio del caos vehicular, después de que el terremoto empujo a miles a las calles en busca de resguardo. Juan Sánchez, un empleado del Ministerio de Economía de 37 años, esperaba un autobús que, según dijo, dudaba que llegara. "Evacuaron todos estos edificios. Todos están afuera. Ahora el problema es, ¿cómo volvemos a casa?", se preguntó. El presidente Raúl Mulino viajó a Penonomé, una ciudad ubicada a medio camino entre el epicentro y Ciudad de Panamá, donde algunos edificios se derrumbaron y una iglesia resultó dañada. A pesar de la fuerza del movimiento telúrico del viernes, el país parece haberse librado de la destrucción causada por otros sismos recientes y potentes en la región. Por el momento, no se reportaron muertos ni heridos. En junio, [USN:L6N42Y0SA TEXT:"dos potentes sismos"] consecutivos en Venezuela causaron la muerte de más de 6,500 personas, mientras que un terremoto en [USN:L1N4480IR TEXT:"Colombia"] en agosto dejó más de 300 fallecidos. Un informe del USGS estimó que alrededor de 43,000 panameños vivían en áreas con al menos una exposición severa al terremoto. Esto se compara con casi 1.4 millones en el área de los dos sismos en Venezuela y más de 1.6 millones en la zona afectada por el terremoto en el oeste de Colombia. VIBRACIONES PROLONGADAS Néstor Luque, director del Instituto de Geociencias de Panamá, atribuyó el sismo al sistema de fallas Azuero-Soná que, según explicó, contiene una enorme acumulación de presión que se libera ocasionalmente. "Las señales sísmicas se propagaron por todo el territorio nacional, por eso se sintió en todas partes", dijo. En Ciudad de Panamá, Luque dijo haber contado 40 segundos de vibraciones, aunque en otras zonas es posible que se hayan sentido temblores aún más prolongados. Sabina Ríos, quien se encontraba en el sexto piso de un antiguo edificio militar estadounidense en Ciudad de Panamá, dijo que el temblor fue inusualmente fuerte y prolongado. "El sismo se sintió fuerte y duró mucho tiempo, el más largo que he sentido en años", dijo Ríos. Víctor Pinzón, un trabajador de mantenimiento de 48 años, dijo a Reuters que había visto a los limpiadores de ventanas de rascacielos soportar el temblor. "Es un milagro que no hayan muerto", dijo. "Parecía que estaban meciéndose en una hamaca", agregó. Los terremotos fuertes no son comunes en Panamá, y algunos ancianos lloraban mientras evacuaban a las calles. "Estamos asustados, solos los dos aquí, la casa se nos rajó y tememos que se nos caiga encima", dijo Ricardo Brown, de 74 años, en una conversación telefónica desde la zona Las Minas, en la provincia de Herrera, al sur de Panamá, donde el sismo dañó varias viviendas. Omar Smith, director de la agencia de protección civil de Panamá, declaró al medio Telemetro que también se habían reportado impactos en Chitré, la capital de Herrera, y en la costa de la provincia de Los Santos.

item.title: Forte terremoto atinge Panamá, mas não causa grandes destruições
item.description: Um terremoto de magnitude 7,7 atingiu o sul do Panamá nesta sexta-feira, causando danos a edifícios e levando milhares de pessoas às ruas, mas o país parece ter escapado de uma destruição generalizada ou de vítimas fatais.
item.dc:creator: Elida Moreno, Dave Sherwood
item.content:encoded: Um terremoto de magnitude 7,7 atingiu o sul do Panamá nesta sexta-feira, causando danos a edifícios e levando milhares de pessoas às ruas, mas o país parece ter escapado de uma destruição generalizada ou de vítimas fatais. O Serviço Geológico dos Estados Unidos informou que o terremoto ocorreu a uma profundidade de 12,6 km, com epicentro em uma área pouco povoada a cerca de 200 km da capital, e que havia possibilidade de algumas vítimas. Nas horas seguintes, mesmo com mais de 40 réplicas abalando o país do istmo, o Canal do Panamá e a mina de cobre Cobre Panamá informaram que as operações estavam normais, e o Aeroporto Internacional de Tocumen revogou a suspensão dos voos. Funcionários de escritórios no sofisticado centro financeiro do centro da Cidade do Panamá se preocupavam em como chegar em casa no meio do engarrafamento, depois que o terremoto levou milhares de pessoas às ruas. Juan Sánchez, um funcionário de 37 anos do Ministério da Economia, esperava por um ônibus que, segundo ele, duvidava que chegaria. “Eles evacuaram todos esses prédios. Todo mundo está na rua. Agora o problema é: como vamos chegar em casa?” O presidente Raúl Mulino viajou para Penonomé, uma cidade localizada a meio caminho entre o epicentro e a Cidade do Panamá, onde alguns prédios desabaram e uma igreja foi danificada. Apesar da intensidade do tremor desta sexta-feira, o país parece ter sido poupado da destruição causada por outros fortes terremotos recentes na região, sem que tenham sido relatadas mortes ou feridos imediatamente. Tremores consecutivos na Venezuela, em junho, mataram vários milhares de pessoas, enquanto um terremoto na Colômbia, em agosto, matou mais de 300. Um relatório de exposição elaborado pelo USGS estimou que cerca de 43 mil panamenhos viviam em áreas com exposição pelo menos grave ao terremoto. Isso se compara a quase 1,4 milhão na área dos terremotos gêmeos na Venezuela e a mais de 1,6 milhão na zona atingida pelo terremoto no oeste da Colômbia. VIBRAÇÕES PROLONGADAS Nestor Luque, diretor do instituto de geociências do Panamá, disse que o terremoto foi desencadeado pelo Sistema de Falhas de Azuero-Sona, que há muito tempo acumulava pressão. “É um sistema de falhas ativas que, ocasionalmente, devido ao acúmulo de tensão, libera essa quantidade de energia”, disse ele. “Os sinais sísmicos se propagaram por todo o território nacional e é por isso que puderam ser sentidos em todos os lugares.” Na Cidade do Panamá, Luque disse ter contado 40 segundos de vibrações, embora outras áreas possam ter sentido tremores ainda mais longos. Sabina Ríos, que estava no sexto andar de um antigo prédio da época da ocupação militar dos EUA na Cidade do Panamá, disse que o tremor foi excepcionalmente forte e prolongado. “O terremoto foi forte e durou muito tempo, o mais longo que senti em anos”, disse Ríos. Víctor Pinzón, um funcionário de manutenção de 48 anos, contou à Reuters que viu limpadores de janelas de arranha-céus resistindo ao tremor. “É um milagre que eles não tenham morrido”, disse ele. “Parecia que estavam balançando em uma rede.” Terremotos fortes não são comuns no Panamá, e alguns moradores idosos choravam enquanto evacuavam para as ruas. “Estamos com medo. Somos só nós dois, idosos, aqui. A casa rachou e temos medo de que ela desabe sobre nós”, disse Ricardo Brown, de 74 anos, na província de Herrera, no sul do Panamá, onde afirmou ter visto várias casas danificadas. Omar Smith, que chefia a agência de proteção civil do Panamá, disse ao veículo de notícias Telemetro Reporta que também foram relatados tremores em Chitre, capital de Herrera, e ao longo da costa na província de Los Santos. O USGS estimou que as perdas econômicas poderiam chegar de 1% a 10% do Produto Interno Bruto do Panamá, e a concessionária de energia Naturgy relatou cortes de energia em seis províncias. O Panamá tinha programado um exercício nacional de retirada para a segunda-feira da próxima semana, a fim de testar as capacidades de resposta a emergências do país em caso de terremotos.

item.title: Strong Panama quake shakes nation, but avoids major destruction
item.description: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.
item.dc:creator: Elida Moreno, Dave Sherwood
item.content:encoded: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths. The US Geological Survey said the earthquake hit at a depth of 12.6 km (7.8 miles), with an epicenter in a sparsely populated area about 200 km (124 miles) from the capital, and that some casualties were possible. In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama Canal and Cobre Panama copper mine reported normal operations and the Tocumen International Airport lifted a suspension on flights. Office workers in the upscale business hub of downtown Panama City fretted about how to get home in the snarl of traffic, after the quake sent thousands into the streets. Juan Sanchez, a 37-year-old economy ministry employee, waited for a bus he said he doubted would arrive. "They evacuated all of these buildings. Everyone is outside. Now the problem is, how do we get home?" President Raul Mulino traveled to Penonome, a city about halfway between the epicenter and Panama City, where some buildings collapsed and a church was damaged. Despite the force of Friday's tremor, the country appeared to have been spared the [USN:L6N44903E TEXT:"destruction"] of other recent powerful quakes in the [USN:L6N42X19G TEXT:"region"], with no deaths or injuries immediately reported. Back-to-back quakes in Venezuela in June killed several thousand people, while a quake in Colombia in August killed more than 300. An exposure report by the USGS estimated about 43,000 Panamanians lived in areas with at least severe exposure to the quake. This compares to nearly 1.4 million in the area of the twin quakes in Venezuela and over 1.6 million in the quake-hit zone of western Colombia. PROLONGED VIBRATIONS Nestor Luque, director of Panama's geosciences institute, attributed the quake to the Azuero Sona Fault System that he said contained a massive buildup of pressure that is occasionally released. "The seismic signals have traveled throughout the national territory and that is why it could be felt everywhere." In Panama City, Luque said he counted 40 seconds of vibrations, though other areas may have felt even longer tremors. Sabina Rios, who was on the sixth floor of an old US military-era building in Panama City, said the shaking was unusually strong and prolonged. "The quake felt strong and lasted a long time, the longest I’ve felt in years,” Rios said. Victor Pinzon, a 48-year-old maintenance worker, told Reuters he had watched high-rise window cleaners ride out the shaking. “It’s a miracle they didn’t get killed,” he said. “They looked like they were swinging in a hammock.” Strong earthquakes are not common in Panama, and some elderly residents were in tears as they evacuated into the streets. “We’re scared. It’s just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we’re afraid it could fall on us,” said Ricardo Brown, 74, in Herrera province in southern Panama, where he said he saw a number of damaged homes. Omar Smith, who heads Panama's civil protection agency, told news outlet Telemetro Reporta that impacts had also been reported in Chitre, the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province. The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to 1% to 10% of Panama's gross domestic product, and electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces. Panama was due to hold a national evacuation drill on Monday of next week to test the country's emergency response.

item.title: Is it legal for the US to livestream the Fort Hood shooter's execution?
item.description: Here's what US law says about public executions and death by firing squad.
item.dc:creator: Jan Wolfe
item.content:encoded: The Pentagon [USN:L1N45U11T TEXT:"said"] on Thursday that it would livestream the firing squad execution of the man who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, raising questions about the legality of the unprecedented announcement. Here's what US law says about public executions and death by firing squad. IS DEATH BY FIRING SQUAD LEGAL IN THE US? Yes. The US Supreme Court said in a unanimous 1879 decision that execution by firing squad is not "cruel and unusual punishment" prohibited by the Constitution. The justices last year cleared the way for South Carolina to carry out its first execution by firing squad in decades. Five states currently allow executions by firing squad: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Utah. The Trump administration earlier this year said it would allow execution by firing squad in the federal prison system. The US Army also once regularly carried out executions by firing squad of US soldiers found guilty of desertion or other offenses. Hundreds of US soldiers were sentenced to death during the Civil War from 1861 to 1865. Under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the president is the only person who can approve a death sentence for a member of the US armed services. President Donald Trump on October 5 signed off on the Pentagon's plan to execute the Fort Hood gunman, Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist. CAN EXECUTIONS BE BROADCAST? Executions in the US were once public spectacles, but in the last century have been carried out in correctional facilities away from the public eye. In 1936, a man convicted of rape was hanged in front of thousands in Owensboro, Kentucky, while the following year, hundreds watched a public hanging in Missouri. A US law prohibits the recording or broadcasting of executions in the federal prison system. But military regulations have not applied that same prohibition to military executions. Hasan was convicted of premeditated murder by a military jury in 2013, following a court-martial trial. State laws regulate who can witness executions, generally limiting access to authorized officials, family members, legal counsel, and a handful of media representatives. Courts have long rejected lawsuits brought by media organizations seeking broader public access to executions. In 2001, a judge denied a request by an internet company to livestream the lethal injection execution of Timothy McVeigh, an anti-government militant who bombed a federal building in Oklahoma City in 1995, killing 168 people. The Justice Department did provide a restricted, closed-circuit television broadcast exclusively for survivors of the bombing and victims' families. COULD HASAN CHALLENGE HIS EXECUTION IN COURT? While Hasan has exhausted his direct appeals within the military justice system, he can still challenge his underlying conviction and sentence in the federal civilian court system. Such a challenge, known as a federal habeas corpus proceeding, provides another layer of review before a death sentence is carried out. Even if unsuccessful, that move could stall the execution, potentially for years. Hasan's execution is currently set for December 3. Hasan could also file a civil rights lawsuit seeking to challenge the method of his execution, legal experts said. Hasan told a panel of military mental health experts in 2010 that he wished he had been killed during the attack because it would have meant God had chosen him for martyrdom, an indication that he may not exercise all his legal options. Hasan acted as his own attorney during his 2013 military trial and offered almost no defense. WHAT ABOUT INTERNATIONAL LAW? The United Nations has condemned the plan to livestream Hasan's execution, saying it is a cruel and inhumane form of punishment that violates an international human rights treaty adopted in 1984 known as the Convention Against Torture. But that treaty, like many other international legal frameworks, is not judicially enforceable within the US court system. "The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture," said the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights.

item.title: Trump says Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets
item.description: His administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, Timothy Gardner, Jarrett Renshaw
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump said on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. Prices for diesel, used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking, are near a record and risk for Trump's fellow Republicans ahead of the November 3 congressional elections that will determine whether they maintain thin control of Congress. Diesel prices fell after the announcement, but analysts said the deal may not be enough to keep them down. Trump said on social media he had a "highly successful" discussion with President Vladimir Putin in which they agreed that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, equal to about 2.25 million barrels of fuel. The US exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day. After the call, an envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, praised cooperation between Russia and the US in a post on X. Dmitriev asked US officials during his visit to Washington last month for licenses to export diesel to the US market to be granted to all Russian major oil firms, sources familiar with the situation said. In October 2025, the US imposed sanctions on Russian oil companies over Moscow's war that began in 2022. The diesel exports could provide Moscow with billions of dollars in revenues that could help Putin continue the war with Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticized the deal, announced while a Ukrainian delegation was in the US to discuss how to seek a resolution of the war, as a "weak decision on the part of strong partners." "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy," he said on X. The deal was also criticized by US lawmakers including Trump's fellow Republican, Representative Don Bacon, who said it is time to apply more sanctions that [USN:L1N4431OK TEXT:"Congress passed recently"], not lift the measures. "Now is the time to use those sanctions to squeeze Putin’s war machine, not reward a dictator by putting more money in his hands while he continues targeting and killing Ukrainian civilians," Bacon said on X. The US Treasury Department issued a license allowing importation of Russian diesel until April 7. Trump said Russia would supply another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Even more would follow, Trump said, "based on the condition of their diesel refineries," which have been damaged by Ukrainian attacks. 'NOTHING BURGER' Analysts said the agreement was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices. "I cannot overstate how much of a nothing burger this is," Rory Johnston, an oil market researcher and founder of CommodityContext.com, said on X, adding that Russia usually exports much more diesel than volumes in the deal when its refinery fleet is not under attack. "It's clearly not a fix, but another stream to aid a very tight diesel market," said Jim Mitchell, an analyst at consultancy Wood Mackenzie. [USN:L1N45U0FQ TEXT:"Diesel prices"], which are often a big driver of inflation, are up 70% since the US and Israel launched the war with Iran on February 28. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have triggered a severe global fuel supply crunch, pushing average US diesel prices to $6.28 a gallon on Thursday, according to the AAA motorist group. Prices have stayed high despite two recent moves by Trump to boost supplies of the fuel: pressuring allies to release emergency reserves and expanding access to tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, which is normally used for farm equipment. US diesel futures fell almost 5% following news of the deal and were trading at $4.64 a gallon. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump said. DEFENSE PRODUCTION ACT Three industry sources said earlier on Friday that Trump will issue a directive in the coming days to some US department heads to find ways to control diesel prices. The directive, which they said could take the form of a presidential memo, will push officials to find ways to bypass local and state regulations blocking energy production and use the Cold War-era Defense Production Act to increase output of oil and fuel. Under the DPA, the president can authorize US-backed loans or loan guarantees to expand domestic manufacturing of critical materials and to require companies to prioritize government contracts for essential goods. The White House has been weighing how to use the DPA to expand refining capacity as the war with Iran exposes US vulnerability to supply disruptions and price spikes. Refining executives [USN:L1N45214P TEXT:"told administration officials"] last month that federal money would be better directed toward making refineries more efficient or expanding plants rather than financing a new refinery, which would be more costly and take years to complete.

item.title: Tesla renames 'Full Self-Driving' to 'Assisted Driving' in Europe as it chases clearance for software
item.description: Several regulators have said the old name is misleading.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: EV-maker Tesla (TSLA.O) has started calling its "Full Self-Driving" feature "Tesla Assisted Driving" on its European websites, dropping a name regulators have said was [USN:L6N41E09R TEXT:"misleading"], as CEO Elon Musk pushes for EU-wide approval for the software. The rebrand comes after Germany said on Tuesday Tesla had [USN:L6N45T0YE TEXT:"offered to switch to the new name"]. Musk has described the self-driving technology as key to the company's future growth. Tesla's FSD page for Slovakia now redirects to a "Tesla Assisted Driving" page, as do pages in other European countries such as Germany, Spain and the Netherlands. The US site still refers to it as "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)." A Reuters [USN:L6N45R0YL TEXT:"report"] published this week detailed how Tesla mounted a campaign to win approval for FSD in Europe, including encouraging owners and supporters to lobby national regulators for faster approvals. In September, a Norwegian Tesla owner asked the Norwegian Public Roads Administration whether Tesla's changes to how it described FSD addressed concerns about the name, according to documents Reuters obtained through freedom-of-information requests. "Please do not simply say again that 'we are waiting for the EU' without explaining what Tesla or Norway must deliver in the meantime," the owner said. Several regulators have said the old name is misleading because the system requires constant supervision and drivers remain legally responsible. In Sweden, consumer protection authorities had earlier asked the Swedish Transport Agency to assess whether the marketing of FSD could give buyers the false impression the system was capable of fully autonomous driving. In Italy, authorities had said in internal government correspondence that the name "Full Self-Driving", together with Tesla's promotional material, "could lead users to believe that the vehicle is equipped with unsupervised automatic driving functions attributable to higher levels of automation, particularly SAE Level 3", in communication seen by Reuters through freedom-of-information requests. Eight EU countries already allow the system, with [USN:L8N45U0I2 TEXT:"Slovakia"] expecting to become the ninth within days. An EU-wide vote has been [USN:L6N45H0TX TEXT:"pushed"] from October to at least December, with countries like France conducting [USN:L6N44V0W3 TEXT:"additional"] testing.

item.title: How the US plan to livestream an execution compares with global practice
item.description: Governments have spent years trying to limit the circulation of violent execution footage.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The U.S. military plans to livestream the Dec. 3 execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting. If carried out as planned, death penalty experts said it would mark the first known broadcast or livestream of a lawful execution. Executions are generally conducted behind prison walls, and internet platforms and governments have spent years trying to limit the circulation of violent execution footage. HAS A LAWFUL EXECUTION EVER BEEN LIVESTREAMED OR BROADCAST TO THE PUBLIC BEFORE? Death penalty experts consulted by Reuters said they were unaware of any previous lawful execution that had been livestreamed or broadcast to a public audience. Execution footage has occasionally emerged after the event. The hanging of former Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein in 2006, for example, was seen around the world after official and unofficial recordings circulated online and through broadcasters, though it was not shown live. Broadcasts and livestreams today are common for court proceedings, parliamentary debates and other state functions, but not for judicial executions. HOW UNUSUAL IS THIS COMPARED WITH MODERN EXECUTION PRACTICES AROUND THE WORLD? Public executions have become rare worldwide, with most countries that retain the death penalty carrying out executions away from public view. According to Amnesty International, public executions recorded in recent years have largely been concentrated in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan. The execution would also be notable in the United States. Public executions largely disappeared during the 20th century, and death penalty experts cited by Reuters said the last legally sanctioned public execution took place in 1936. Hasan's execution would be the first carried out by firing squad by the U.S. military since the 1945 execution of Eddie Slovik, who was convicted of desertion during World War Two. HOW HAS THE INTERNET CHANGED THE CIRCULATION OF EXECUTION FOOTAGE? The internet has transformed execution imagery from a local event into content capable of reaching global audiences within minutes. Militant groups such as Islamic State became notorious for producing professionally edited execution videos that were distributed online as propaganda and recruitment tools. Criminal organisations, including Mexican drug cartels, have also circulated violent footage to intimidate rivals and project power. The ability of users to rapidly copy, repost and redistribute content has made it more difficult for governments and technology companies to control the spread of such material. WHAT HAS BEEN THE REACTION FROM GOVERNMENTS AND TECH COMPANIES? Governments and technology companies have generally moved in the opposite direction, attempting to reduce rather than expand access to graphic execution footage. Major social media platforms have spent years removing execution videos linked to extremist organisations and other violent groups. One of the first public governmental reactions came from New Zealand, whose chief censor said authorities would have little practical ability to prevent residents from accessing a livestream while it was taking place. Livestreams pose particular challenges for platforms because footage can be viewed, copied and redistributed before moderation systems can intervene. Even countries that still conduct public executions have often restricted filming and broadcast rights. Saudi Arabia historically carried out public executions before spectators, but recording them was prohibited and such public executions had largely ceased by 2019. (This story has been corrected to fix the year to 2001, not 2021, in paragraph 15.)

item.title: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
item.description: Navi Pillay sat in the court's appeals chamber.
item.dc:creator: Humeyra Pamuk, Steve Holland, Anthony Deutsch
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, hours after one of its [USN:L8N45V0JG TEXT:"former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize"], putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies. The court denounced the move as an "assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," and called on its 125 member states to take action to defend it. "The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it," it said in a statement. "This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law. History will judge this moment." The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court, founded in 2002 [USN:L6N3VQ0DE TEXT:"to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide"], and has previously [USN:O8N42O02H TEXT:"imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges"]. Friday's move goes much further, potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself, amounting to an unprecedented attack on an institution founded on an international treaty. The US initially signed the Rome Statute that founded the court but never ratified it. "President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement, first published by Reuters. "That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate." SANCTIONS INCLUDE GRACE PERIOD The US Treasury announced the sanctions with a six-month initial grace period, and some other exemptions that would allow some transactions for telecoms, software, payment of pensions and transactions related to detainees. Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns, and would be adjusted if those demands were not met. Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and an investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC says is "deprioritized." Rubio in his statement cited calls from outside experts for the ICC to prosecute American service members, border patrol agents and elected leaders. ICC officials have not taken steps toward such prosecutions. "The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan told Reuters. "Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions." EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on social media that the six-month period "offers a window for dialogue" but added that the bloc "has options to ensure that (the ICC) can continue its vital work." Belgium's foreign minister called for an EU blocking statute to be activated to protect the court. The ICC has issued arrest warrants against more than 70 people, including world leaders and major figures in global conflicts. In addition to Netanyahu, it has sought the arrest of Hamas figures. Others who were the subject of arrest warrants include Russian President Vladimir Putin, former Sudan President Omar al-Bashir and former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi. Charges against Kenyan President William Ruto and former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta were withdrawn. NOBEL COMMITTEE CITES POLITICAL ATTACKS IN AWARDING PRIZE Despite [USN:L6N45G1AB TEXT:"US calls for countries to quit the court"], it has received strong backing from most member states, which include all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the United States and Turkey. It is based in the Netherlands, an EU and NATO member. The Nobel Prize awarded hours earlier to South African jurist Navi Pillay, who sat on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003-2008, was explicitly described by the prize committee as a gesture of support for such tribunals at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack". "An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world," the prize committee said. US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organization, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation. The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during his first term, which were rescinded under President Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025. Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of [USN:L6N45D0HW TEXT:"sanctions on the court"] itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.

item.title: China, EU strike deal to halve Chinese hybrid exports
item.description: Shares of European carmakers, which have slid steadily over the past two years, broadly gained on the news.
item.dc:creator: Joe Cash
item.content:encoded: China and the European Union have reached a deal that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the bloc by more than half, European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said on Friday after talks in Beijing aimed at reducing the EU's ballooning trade deficit with China. The "shared understanding" would "moderate" China's export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU, and would cut the imports of several million cars over four years, Sefcovic said after the two-day talks, without offering details on how the agreement will be implemented. Shares of European carmakers, which have slid steadily over the past two years due to US tariffs and soaring Chinese exports, broadly gained on the news. The understanding came after discussions between Sefcovic and Chinese officials including Commerce Minister Wang Wentao over three months, and comes after years of disputes between Beijing and Brussels over soaring Chinese exports, such as cars. EU leaders will discuss the outcome at the start of their summit in Brussels next Thursday to determine whether the agreement marks the start of a rebalancing of the bloc's trade deficit with China that has swelled to more than €1 billion ($1.12 billion) a day. Sefcovic said he believed the two sides had achieved a very good result. "Having said that, this is far from the end. It is a crucial first step – but only a first step – in the process of rebalancing," he told reporters in Beijing. Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament's trade committee, said the hybrid deal needed to extend to other sectors as well and that the EU should also deploy trade defence measures more effectively. Chinese Commerce Minister Wang told Sefcovic that China was not the root cause of the EU's problems, but a partner in solving them, according to the Chinese ministry. The two sides also reached understandings on reducing Chinese import duties on some €4 billion of EU exports, including car parts, olive oil and footwear, and on smoothing China's granting of export licences for rare earths and permanent magnets, Sefcovic said. CHINESE CAR IMPORTS TO EU SURGE EU governments are alarmed by the sharp rise in car imports from China as their own carmakers lay off workers, notably at Volkswagen (VOWG.DE) where [USN:L8N44W0B8 TEXT:"100,000 job are going"]. Imports of plug-in hybrids into the EU increased 86% in the year to September, with a 20% decline in prices. More than half of these vehicles are now from China, while for 2025, China's share of plug-in hybrid electric vehicle imports was 30% in value terms. China and the EU's dispute over cheap Chinese EV exports, resulting in EU tariffs in 2024, has clouded bilateral ties, and has since broadened to include Chinese measures against EU brandy, pork and dairy, as well as Chinese restrictions on exports of rare earths and critical minerals. Paris and Berlin are among the hardest hit by Beijing's measures, with France accounting for 90% of EU brandy exports to China and Germany heavily exposed in dairy. China and the EU said in their joint statement they would continue discussions on price undertakings as an alternative to tariffs. However, even with the tariffs, Chinese EV exports have started to increase again this year. German auto industry group [USN:S8N43B03D TEXT:"VDA"] cautiously welcomed the agreement, but said it was too early to determine if it would address unfair competition. Mercedes-Benz (MBGn.DE) said the deal showed constructive dialogue was the right way to address challenges and it should provide greater predictability. Matthias Schmidt, European autos research analyst, said countries like Germany had thought themselves immune to the threat from Chinese car companies, but were waking up and asking Brussels to step in. "The result is this statement from Sefcovic today," he said. "Now Berlin is asking London to join them, and Brussels, given the UK accounts for 30% of Western Europe’s Chinese new car sales." As part of Friday's agreement, China's commerce ministry said it also would continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets through a "green channel" mechanism. TRADE IMBALANCE AT HEART OF DISPUTE Chinese exports to the EU totalled $560 billion last year, according to UN Comtrade data, up from $517 billion in 2024, as exports to major economies including Germany, Italy, Spain and Poland each rose about 10% from a year earlier, while shipments to Hungary jumped 43%. Meanwhile, China took $268.3 billion worth of European goods last year, down from $269.4 billion a year prior, led by purchases from Denmark, Ireland and France. China needs foreign buyers for the flood of relatively cheap state-subsidised goods its own shoppers can't absorb, and the EU is torn between welcoming those imports to ease living costs and keeping them out to rebuild its own factories. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned the European Parliament last month that the trade gap had reached a tipping point and that the 27-member bloc would use all the tools at its disposal to rebalance the relationship. China and the EU will keep exploring the possibility of lowering tariffs on certain goods and continue dialogue on market access for medical devices, the Chinese ministry said. Sefcovic and Wang are set to meet again in March 2027, with a video conference call in January. ($1 = 0.8920 euros)

item.title: TSX posts biggest gain in five weeks as rate hike bets recede
item.description: Canada's main stock index rose on Friday by the most in five weeks, led by gains for Aritzia and metal mining shares, as weaker-than-expected domestic jobs data reduced expectations for Bank of Canada interest rate hikes.
item.dc:creator: Fergal Smith
item.content:encoded: Canada's main stock index rose on Friday by the most in five weeks, led by gains for Aritzia and metal mining shares, as weaker-than-expected domestic jobs data reduced expectations for Bank of Canada interest rate hikes. The Toronto Stock Exchange's S&P/TSX Composite Index (.GSPTSE) ended up 519.24 points, or 1.48%, at 35,664.62, marking its highest closing level in two weeks and its biggest advance since September 3. For the week, the index added 0.46% after two straight weeks of declines. "Markets didn't want to end three weeks down in a row." said Ben Jang, a portfolio manager at Nicola Wealth. "It's the same story - bad news for the economy, good news for valuations." Canada's economy shed 68,300 jobs in September and the unemployment rate edged up to 6.5%. Analysts had forecast a jobs gain of 9,200. "The market has been quite hawkish and pricing in hikes which now, with such a weak job number, likely means a pause in that process," Jang said. Investors see a 25% chance the BoC would hike at the October 28 policy announcement, down from 40% before the jobs report. Lower interest rates increase the value to investors of the cash flows companies are expected to earn. The materials sector (.GSPTTMT) , which includes metal mining shares, rose 2.81% as bargain buying emerged for [USN:L1N45V0M5 TEXT:"gold"] after bullion touched a two-month low earlier this week. Energy (.SPTTEN) was up 1.07% as oil recouped its earlier declines. US crude oil futures settled 0.4% higher at $91.85 a barrel. Shares of [USN:TUA4XWXNP TEXT:"Aritzia"] (ATZ.TO) surged more than 20% after the apparel retailer topped analyst expectations for second-quarter revenue and profit. That helped lift the consumer discretionary sector (.GSPTTCD) by 2.66%. Technology (.SPTTTK) rose 2.88% and heavily weighted financials ended 1.21% higher. Communication services stocks were a drag, with Cogeco Communications (CCA.TO) falling 7.11% and BCE (BCE.TO) down 5.47%. US and European telecom stocks also tumbled after [USN:L4N45V0L0 TEXT:"SpaceX's acquisition "]of low-band spectrum heightened concerns over growing competition from satellite-based mobile services.

item.title: AI-centered US stock bull market nears four-year anniversary
item.description: The US bull market is going strong as it nears its four-year anniversary, driven by an AI spending engine that is propelling corporate profits and economic growth.
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf
item.content:encoded: The US bull market is going strong as it nears its four-year anniversary, driven by an AI spending engine that is propelling corporate profits and economic growth. The S&P 500 (.SPX) is trading around record-high levels ahead of October 12, which will mark four years since the benchmark stock index's closing low for this cycle — signaling the start of the latest bull run. Sizzling corporate profit growth — lifted by spending on the AI expansion and a solid economic backdrop — has helped drive the latest leg of the market's rally and is a primary reason for investor optimism in coming quarters. But even as the index climbs, risks loom. The Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes and spiking US Treasury yields both provide obstacles that could sap the momentum for equities. Markets could be volatile heading into next month's [USN:L4N44V1HA TEXT:"US midterm elections."] The market's dependence on AI also presents a worry, with any hints of weakness in the trend possibly met with severe punishment. "The AI theme is the defining feature of this bull market," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise. "What you're seeing in terms of the bull market four years in is, I think, the easy money around AI has been made ... as we get further into this bull market, there is just going to be more pressure on especially technology companies to prove that the spending that they're doing today is actually going to translate into the profits." CURRENT RUN RANKS MIDDLE-AGED AMONG BULLS As bull markets go, the current one could be classified as middle-aged. The S&P 500's latest run ranks as the eighth-longest bull market since World War Two, according to Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group. While stock experts differ on defining a bull market, a common definition is a gain of at least 20% that has followed a decline of at least 20% from a peak. The current bull run has tallied a gain of 117%, which is the sixth-best-performing bull market since World War Two. "Four years is not, by any stretch of the imagination, scary with regards to a bull market," said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist for Nationwide. "They don't end of old age; they end from disease." TECH, AI AT HEART OF BULL RUN AI has dominated the latest bull run, with the launch of ChatGPT coming about a month after the bull market began. US companies are posting massive profit growth, with S&P 500 earnings expected to rise more than 35% this year, boosted by capital spending from "hyperscalers" to build data centers. Oxford Economics estimates about one-third of recent US economic growth stems from AI, including the net impact of direct investment to support expansion of AI infrastructure as well as some contribution from the wealth effect from stock market gains lifting consumer spending. "You're seeing that AI theme show up in the economy and in corporate profits," Saglimbene said. Of the 11 S&P 500 sectors, only technology and communication services — which includes megacap AI players Alphabet (GOOGL.O) and Meta Platforms (META.O) — have posted stronger gains than the index itself during the bull run. The market capitalization of Nvidia (NVDA.O) — whose AI chips have made the company the poster child of this technological era — has soared to $5.8 trillion from $286 billion on October 12, 2022. It has become the largest company by market value in the world. Thirteen US companies boast market values of at least $1 trillion — all but two either in the tech sector or with significant AI exposure. CONCENTRATION RISK GROWS WITH TECH DOMINANCE The gains in massive tech and AI stocks give them more significant sway over major stock indexes, but also make them top-heavy. The weight of the top 10 companies in the S&P 500 has grown to about 40% from about 28% in October 2022, according to J.P. Morgan Asset Management. "It is a reflection of fundamental strength and earnings outperformance, but also it introduces some risks," said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global investment strategist at Edward Jones. "The risk of concentration is that if the prevailing theme goes out of favor, portfolios might feel it in an outsized way." Another risk is the Fed's recent pivot to rate hikes, as the US central bank seeks to bring down high inflation. Tighter monetary policy could slow the economy, perhaps severely. Indeed, the last bear market that led to the low in October 2022 coincided with a sharp rate-hiking cycle. Rate hikes also factor in to the huge jump in Treasury yields. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was hovering at around 5.2%, after recently reaching its highest level in 24 years. Higher yields pose headwinds for equities, including potentially greater investment competition from bonds. Kourkafas said Edward Jones remains overweight equities but the recommendation is less aggressive than it was before, with the strategist noting the increasing attractiveness of fixed income. "We still think that the bull market is not about to end ... but it makes sense to us to take some of the risk off the table," he said.

item.title: Hurricane Simon strengthens off Mexico's Pacific coast, threatens tourist region
item.description: Hurricane Simon is rapidly intensifying off Mexico's Pacific coast, packing sustained winds of 110 mph (177 kph) as it churns toward a stretch of coastline dotted with beach resorts and fishing towns, the US National Hurricane Center said on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Becerril
item.content:encoded: Hurricane Simon is rapidly intensifying off Mexico's Pacific coast, packing sustained winds of 110 mph (177 kph) as it churns toward a stretch of coastline dotted with beach resorts and fishing towns, the US National Hurricane Center said on Friday. Simon, nearing Category 3 strength, is forecast to become a dangerous Category 4 by Saturday as it approaches Mexico's southwestern and west-central Pacific coast, one of the country's most popular tourist regions, the NHC said. "Simon could deliver the most significant hurricane impact to this stretch of the Mexican Pacific coast since Lidia in 2023, which damaged thousands of homes and devastated crops along the Jalisco coast," said Tyler Roys, a senior meteorologist at AccuWeather. Simon is expected to make landfall on Sunday between Manzanillo — Mexico’s largest port and the main gateway for trade with Asia — and Puerto Vallarta, a popular beach destination and home to nearly 300,000 residents. In Manzanillo, fishermen were hauling their boats off the beach and authorities were putting up black flags along the coast to signal the beach was closed. The Mexican Navy activated emergency response personnel in Colima and restricted maritime traffic along parts of the Pacific coast, closing ports to smaller vessels and barring larger vessels from operating in Michoacan. Simon was about 195 miles (315 km) south of Manzanillo in the afternoon and crawling northwest, according to the NHC. Forecasters warned that Simon could bring life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with isolated rainfall totals reaching 30 inches (762 mm) in parts of Michoacan, Colima, Jalisco and Nayarit. Mexican authorities warned that heavy rainfall was expected in the states of Guerrero, Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco.
